Known issues: (1) several agents repeat the claim that Orbyte lists "follow up unpaid invoices" on its roadmap; this is overstated, see docs/research/01-pain-research-shortlist.md. candidates.title: Late-paying B2B customers lock up earned cash, and chasing it is manual
candidates.description: Micro and small B2B suppliers deliver first and get paid about two months later. Experian puts the SME average at 64 days in early 2025, against 58 days for large corporates. MAMBA (via FocusM) says micro and small firms wait 60-120 days. Meanwhile payroll, rent and supplier bills fall due monthly. Cash buffers are thin, and micro firms are named as the most exposed group. The surveys conflict, though: Samenta reports 70% of SMEs with under 6 months of reserves, while SME Bank 1H 2026 reports 70% with MORE than 6 months. Quote neither figure without the other. Malaysia has no statutory late-payment interest regime. Small claims are capped at RM5,000, and a company cannot self-represent. So collection comes down to owners chasing by WhatsApp and phone. Two October 2026 signals: the KUSKOP minister hoped Budget 2027 would bring stronger late-payment protection, and Insap said the budget does not fix cash flow. Orbyte's platform page lists 'follow up unpaid invoices' only as future direction, not as a shipped module. The thin-cash-buffer and cash-runway pain is merged in here as the consequence of this pain.
candidates.who: Micro and small B2B suppliers on 30-90 day credit terms. Includes transport/logistics, wholesale/trading, hospitality and catering suppliers, B2B services, printers, small manufacturers, and suppliers to corporates, GLCs and government. Experian, Samenta and SMEAM figures cover all SMEs, including medium firms. No source splits out micro firms.
candidates.frequency: Continuous: every credit invoice. Chasing overdue accounts is weekly. Collisions with payroll, rent and supplier dates are monthly.
candidates.money_impact: SME delay is 64 days on average (Experian, May 2025). Transport/logistics averages 76 days, and its SME-vs-corporate gap was 26 days in 1Q 2025. MAMBA puts micro/small waits at 60-120 days. Only 9.8% of SMEAM respondents said their cash flow was healthy (NST, Jul 2026). No ringgit loss per micro firm was found.
candidates.deadline_or_penalty: Indirect but forced. Salaries, EPF, rent, supplier and loan payments still fall due. Unpaid rural-road contractors closed or were sued by their suppliers (The Vibes, Sep 2026). There is no statutory late-interest lever (Allianz Trade, snippet only).
candidates.already_spending: Firms borrow to bridge the gap: 51% of MSMEs name working capital as their primary funding need (SME Bank 1H 2026), and BNM's SRF has approved more than RM1.7bil. Factoring is under-used (MAMBA). Lawyers' letters of demand are used in bad cases. Owner time spent chasing is NOT quantified in any source.

evidence.what_it_says: SME payment delays fell from 69 days (2022) to 64 days in early 2025. Large corporations averaged 58 days. The 1Q 2025 SME-corporate gap was 26 days in transport/logistics, 13 in hospitality and 10 in wholesale. Transport/logistics averaged 76 days. CEO: 'many SMEs remain highly exposed to cash flow gaps.' Not split by micro or small.

evidence.source: FocusM quoting MAMBA secretary-general Alvin Low
evidence.what_it_says: Micro and small firms 'often deliver products and services upfront but only receive payment 60 to 120 days later'. That makes it hard to cover salaries and 'replenish inventory'. Factoring is 'under-utilised'. This is the article's framing, not a measured statistic.

evidence.source: The Star quoting think tank Insap
evidence.what_it_says: Budget 2027 'still does not address the core problem of cash flow'. 'The pressing question is whether they can pay suppliers, rent and salaries in the coming months.'
KUSKOP minister Steven Sim hoped Budget 2027 would bring progress on 'strengthening late-payment protection' for SMEs. Reported indirectly, not as a direct quote.

evidence.source: The Star interview with BNM Assistant Governor Suhaimi Ali
evidence.what_it_says: SRF applicants say 'supply-chain delays, extra inventory requirements, and slower customer payments' raised working-capital needs. More than RM1.7bil approved for 2,789 SMEs as at 10 July 2026.
DPM criticised non-payment of rural-road contractors who had finished their work. Some closed, and others were sued by material suppliers and subcontractors.

evidence.source: The Star quoting SMEAM's Chin Chee Seong and Samenta's William Ng
evidence.what_it_says: Many SMEs can operate about 3-6 months if conditions stay challenging. Micro firms have even tighter buffers. 'a significant proportion of micro and small firms may face critical operational distress within three to six months.'

evidence.source: FMT quoting the Samenta SME Outlook Survey 2025/26
evidence.what_it_says: '70% of SMEs had less than six months' worth of cash reserves'. 'Nearly 30% of SMEs still operate manually'.

evidence.source: NST / SME Bank SME Sentiment Index 1H 2026 (search summary; body not extracted)
evidence.what_it_says: The SSI hit a record low of 45.1. 70% of MSMEs report MORE than six months of reserves, 'although micro enterprises remain more vulnerable'. 51% name working-capital financing as their primary need. Conflicts with Samenta's 70% under six months.

evidence.source: NST on an SME Association of Malaysia survey
evidence.what_it_says: Only 9.8% of respondents called their cash flow healthy. 49% said they were under pressure and may need financing support.
'Collecting payment is always an issue. Always 30 days became 60/90/120 days.' 'kononnya big company but owe me money for more than 2 months still havent pay.'

evidence.source: Funding Societies (REGIONAL survey, about 1,000 SMEs in 5 SEA countries)
evidence.what_it_says: Following up on late payments was the most widespread receivables issue in the region. Manual reminders lead to neglected follow-ups. Gives no Malaysia percentages.

evidence.source: Allianz Trade country page (search snippet only)
evidence.what_it_says: Malaysian law 'provides no framework when it comes to late payment'. Interest must be set in the contract.
Small claims cover a 'debt of RM 5,000.00 or less' and take 3-4 months. A company cannot self-represent.

evidence.source: The Star on an Airwallex-commissioned survey (415 SMEs, H1 2026; vendor)
evidence.what_it_says: 42% cite 'managing local and global cash flow' as a key pressure.
Lists 'follow up unpaid invoices' and a Business Graph linking invoices, payment terms and cash flow, framed as future direction, not shipped features.

super_pain_test.money: pass: cash locked about 64 days on average (60-120 for micro per MAMBA); contractor closures documented
super_pain_test.already_spending: partial: financing and factoring costs and lawyers are evidenced; owner chasing time is not quantified
super_pain_test.deadline_or_penalty: partial: no statutory late interest, but payroll, rent and supplier due dates force the consequence monthly
super_pain_test.frequency: pass: every credit invoice; chasing is weekly

candidates.scope_flags: Not HR/admin. It must not process real payments: a payment link or confirmation must be simulated. It must not draft legal letters of demand as legal advice; reminders and escalation to a human are fine. Size caveat: the headline statistics cover SMEs including medium firms. Orbyte overlap: 'follow up unpaid invoices' is on Orbyte's stated roadmap, not live. That is good for hub fit, but the team should position it as the module that delivers that roadmap item.
candidates.why_ranked_here: Strongest and most recent Malaysian evidence: Experian trade data, BNM, SME associations, a minister, a think tank and owner voice, with October 2026 relevance. It passes money and frequency. It maps cleanly to the brief's journey: invoice overdue trigger, then invoice, terms and payment history, then a rule-based reminder tier, then owner approval before a firm or final reminder, then sent, logged and shown on a cash-runway view. It fits Orbyte's own roadmap without duplicating a live module. Weak points: no micro-only data and no quantified chasing time.

candidates.title: Orders taken over WhatsApp with no buyer verification or deposit: fake 'government' bulk orders and vanishing customers
candidates.description: Caterers, bakeries, kuih sellers, gift and flower shops and printing shops take large orders by WhatsApp or phone with no structured check. Pattern (a) is a syndicate. A buyer poses as a government agency, police HQ or ministry, sometimes with a forged Local Order (LO). They order a big batch, ask for extra items the business does not make, and refer the owner to a fake 'supplier'. That supplier demands upfront payment into mule accounts, then everyone disappears. Bukit Aman counted 241 such souvenir and food-supply cases (over RM8 million) in 2025, and 80 cases (RM1.9 million) by May 2026. Pattern (b) is real or fake consumers who refuse a deposit, then cancel or vanish after the food is made, or 'pay later' and never do. Police advice each time is the same manual checklist: verify the buyer through official channels, meet in person, take a deposit, and do not prepay unknown suppliers. That checklist is exactly what a workflow can enforce.
candidates.who: Micro and small caterers, bakeries, kuih and home-based food sellers, gift, flower and souvenir shops, printing and stationery shops, and small traders that sell to government agencies. Peaks at Ramadan/Raya and event seasons. All evidence is Malaysian, and the victims are clearly micro firms.
candidates.frequency: Order intake and screening is daily or weekly. Fraud hits any one business only occasionally: nationally 241 reported cases in 2025, about 4-5 per week. Consumer cancellations recur weekly in festive peaks.
candidates.money_impact: RM300 (a cancelled doughnut order) to RM315,963 (one Raub printing shop's business savings, 2026). Seven Perak bakery and caterer cases exceeded RM300,000. Five Kuantan traders lost RM89,300. National total over RM8 million in 2025 (souvenir plus food-supply scams combined).
candidates.deadline_or_penalty: Food is cooked for a fixed event date and is wasted if the buyer vanishes. Transfers to mule accounts are effectively irreversible. Event urgency pressures owners to pay the fake supplier fast.
candidates.already_spending: Unknown or none evidenced. Owners absorb losses and file police reports. No source shows spending on verification tools. Manual verification costs owner time.

evidence.what_it_says: 241 cases in 2025 with losses over RM8 million, and 80 cases so far in 2026 with RM1.9 million. Suspects pose as government agencies or companies and place bulk orders for souvenirs or food supplies.

Seven reports from bakeries and caterers, with losses over RM300,000. Scammers ask for extra items 'usually ones not produced by the business operator' and refer victims to a supplier demanding upfront payment.

A Raub photocopy/printer business owner lost RM315,963 of 'the victim's business savings'. A fake PPD Kuala Kangsar contact sent an LO and named a fake supplier. Her request for the supplier's registration and TIN got no response.
Five Kuantan traders lost RM89,300. The scammers used a forged LO and vendor appointment letters and directed payment to private accounts. Police: 'a consistent modus operandi across the cases'.

Five small flower and gift traders in Miri lost more than RM28,000 to fake 'door gift' orders. Payments went to mule accounts. Police advise confirming by phone or in person, and warn that letterheads can be forged.

evidence.source: Malay Mail (headline and search summary; fetch returned 403)
evidence.what_it_says: Two caterers lost RM8,800 to a syndicate using the Johor police HQ's name.
A trader lost over RM175,000 on a fictitious order linked to the Youth and Sports Ministry. Not fetched.
66 cases recorded in Perak since the previous year. Police advise wariness about unusual orders, meeting in person and taking deposits. Unverified: not opened.
A Penampang caterer made 150 lunch sets for a fake 'army officer' who refused a deposit, then blocked her. She took no deposit because 'government orders are typically paid only after fulfilment'.
A home seller made RM300 of doughnuts. The customer refused a deposit and cancelled at delivery.
George Town cookie sellers report last-minute cancellations and customers blocking their number. A bakery switched to 'booking with payment' to avoid double losses.
A home kuih seller chased a RM5 debt for days. A commenter said the owed total reached nearly RM100 before the seller gave up.

super_pain_test.money: pass: RM8m+ nationally in 2025; single cases up to RM315,963; micro victims
super_pain_test.already_spending: fail/unknown: no evidence of paid tools; losses absorbed; manual checks only
super_pain_test.deadline_or_penalty: pass: irreversible mule transfers; perishable food wasted on a fixed event date
super_pain_test.frequency: partial: order screening is daily or weekly, but fraud hits each business rarely; consumer cancellations weekly at peaks

candidates.scope_flags: No HR/admin overlap. Must not process payments: deposit requests and supplier-payment holds are simulated. Not legal advice. Clearly a micro/small problem. Note: the anti-scam angle could drift toward a generic 'scam checker' chatbot, which the rubric penalises. Keep it as an order-intake workflow with red-flag rules and an approval gate.
candidates.why_ranked_here: Strong, recent, quantified Malaysian evidence from police, national and regional outlets, with micro firms clearly the victims. It fits the brief's journey well: a WhatsApp order arrives, then buyer details, order history and the item-vs-catalogue check are pulled together, then explainable red-flag rules fire (impersonated agency, items outside the catalogue, referral to a third-party supplier, refused deposit), then the owner must approve before cooking starts or any supplier prepayment, then the order is accepted or held and logged. Ranked below P1 because it fails the 'already spending' test and each business is hit only occasionally.

candidates.title: Payment 'confirmed' by screenshot: fake transfer receipts and swapped QR codes mean goods leave unpaid
candidates.description: Counters, bazaar stalls and WhatsApp/Facebook sellers accept DuitNow QR and bank transfers but confirm payment by eye, using a screenshot or the customer's 'successful' screen. Checking the bank app for each sale gets skipped when busy. Fraudsters exploit this in four ways: edited receipts, 1-sen transfers edited to look like the full amount, 'request for money' notifications shown as payments, and reused proof images. A variant pastes the fraudster's QR sticker over the merchant's DuitNow code. Owners discover the loss only at end-of-day checks or later. The real gap is no fast match between claimed payments and actual credits before goods or shipments are released. Bukit Aman QR-fraud totals (RM40.85mil in 2025) are NOT split by victim type and must not be quoted as merchant losses.
candidates.who: Micro retailers, mini-markets, pasar malam and Ramadan bazaar stalls, hawkers and restaurants taking QR or transfer payments. Chat-based sellers who ship after a screenshot. Also B2B supplier companies (one syndicate case).
candidates.frequency: Exposure on every transfer or QR sale, daily. Publicised incidents recur through 2024-2025 and peak in Ramadan. One alleged case ran about 200 fake receipts over 8 months.
candidates.money_impact: Typical incidents run RM54-RM780. RM300 was described as 'a week of staff wages' for a small shop. Outliers: an alleged RM246,611 over 8 months (kunafa business) and a RM166,338.10 syndicate against suppliers (6 cases). One bazaar stall received only about half its expected QR sales. No aggregate merchant figure exists.
candidates.deadline_or_penalty: Immediate and usually final: goods leave on the spot. Recovery depends on CCTV, viral posts or police.
candidates.already_spending: Partial. Staff and owner time checking bank apps. Police-linked advice to buy DuitNow QR soundboxes (search summary). Payment terminals with sound alerts. No tool spend figure.

evidence.what_it_says: A Port Dickson supermarket lost RM780 of goods to a fake 'successful' receipt. 'there was no credit transaction — just a request for money notification.' The payment had not been verified immediately.
A cosmetics shop lost RM300 to an edited QR receipt. Owner: 'untuk kami peniaga kecil boleh cover bayar gaji seminggu'. The edit was hard to notice at a glance.

evidence.source: SAYS Seismik citing traders' X posts
evidence.what_it_says: A bazaar kuih stall: 'Cuma separuh je yang masuk.' A nasi kerabu seller says a customer reused the same payment proof for a second, unpaid purchase.
A one-sen transfer with an edited receipt was used to buy a RM54 watch at a pasar malam. The suspect said a friend had succeeded several times.
A kunafa business alleges RM246,611 lost to edited receipts over eight months, about 200 receipts. RM69,300 repaid so far.
A Jerantut murtabak stall handed over 50 murtabak (RM400) after a QR payment that never went through. Noticed only after breaking fast.
Selangor police broke a syndicate using fake receipts against supplier companies: six cases, RM166,338.10.
Shah Alam: a RM304.50 receipt screenshot, but 'no such payment had been transacted'. Two cases totalled RM348.10.
A man stuck his own QR over a KL restaurant's counter code. It was caught when a customer's payment did not arrive. A similar incident in Rawang the day before.

evidence.source: The Star citing Bukit Aman CCID
evidence.what_it_says: QR fraud: 5,907 cases / RM40.85mil in 2025 and 5,134 / RM28.67mil in Jan-Jun 2026. CAVEAT: describes 'quishing' and does NOT say whether victims are merchants. Not a merchant-loss figure.
A police-linked advisory calls fake receipts a common tactic against traders and suggests DuitNow QR soundboxes.
Fake payment receipts can be generated with AI or bought. Advice: soundboxes and verifying each transaction.
Lists fake payment proof on Facebook Marketplace and WhatsApp as a common scam against sellers: 'Never rely on screenshots alone.' No statistics.
Small sellers often confirm payment via WhatsApp screenshots, which are easy to fake. Its RM8,500 example is illustrative, not a reported case.

super_pain_test.money: partial: mostly RM54-RM780 per incident, with documented outliers of RM166k-RM246k; no aggregate merchant figure
super_pain_test.already_spending: partial: staff time on bank-app checks; soundboxes suggested (unverified spend)
super_pain_test.deadline_or_penalty: pass: goods leave immediately; loss is final
super_pain_test.frequency: pass: exposure on every transfer sale, daily

candidates.scope_flags: Close to the 'processing real payments' boundary. The product may only read and match (synthetic) credit notifications, and must never move money. In real life it would need a bank or DuitNow notification feed through an Orbyte Connect partner, which is the team's hardest dependency risk. Competition: DuitNow soundboxes and bank push notifications already partly solve the counter case. A human approval step is awkward at a busy counter, so a better demo is the chat-seller flow: hold shipment until the credit matches, then staff approve release. Not HR.
candidates.why_ranked_here: Many independent Malaysian reports, a micro-specific victim base, daily exposure and final losses. It is a natural trigger-to-match-to-approve-release journey with an end-of-day claimed-vs-received reconciliation log. Ranked below P1 and P2 because per-incident amounts are mostly small, aggregate merchant data is missing, existing soundboxes overlap, and real deployment depends on bank data access.

candidates.title: Input costs and supplier prices rise faster than owners can see the margin hit and reprice
candidates.description: Rising costs top every 2024-2026 Malaysian SME survey found. Drivers include materials, utilities, rent, wages, logistics, SST and, in 2026, fuel and energy shocks from the West Asia conflict. In F&B, single ingredients doubled or tripled within weeks (late-2025 monsoon), and the egg subsidy ended in Aug 2025. Owners mostly absorb the rise, buy only 1-2 days of stock, shrink portions and reprice late. Any price change must also appear on price tags and menus, and KPDN compounds traders for missing price displays. Caveat: cost pressure is very well evidenced, but the claim that owners lack per-item margin visibility is INFERRED. No survey measures it.
candidates.who: Micro and small F&B (kopitiam, mamak, tomyam, stalls, caterers, cafes, home bakers), retail, manufacturing, construction and services. SMEAM names manufacturing as most concerned.
candidates.frequency: Continuous. Supplier prices change weekly in F&B with daily purchasing. Utilities and payroll reset monthly.
candidates.money_impact: SMEAM Oct 2026 (n=333): 76.9% expect significantly higher operating costs, 59.5% lower margins and 57.4% may have to raise prices. SMEAM Jul 2026: 83.3% saw cost increases above 10%, and 63.7% above 30%. ACCCIM 2025: 79.5% higher costs and 67.8% reduced margins after the SST expansion. Tomyam operators: ingredients up 10-20% in H1 2025. Mustard greens went from RM2.50-3 to RM6-7/kg in two months (NST, Dec 2025).
candidates.deadline_or_penalty: No hard deadline. Margin erosion leads to losses or closure. KPDN price-display compounds (RM200-RM300 eatery examples; 123 cases / RM13,300 in Johor Raya 2025, not eatery-specific). Scrutiny under the Anti-Profiteering Act. Over-buying perishables means spoilage.
candidates.already_spending: Partial. Widespread cost-cutting: one in two businesses (UOB 2025). Owner time spent sourcing and repricing. No evidence of paid costing tools among micro firms.

evidence.source: Malay Mail on the SMEAM Quick Business Survey (333 responses)
evidence.what_it_says: 61.6% say conditions are worse than 12 months ago. 76.9% expect significantly higher operating costs, 59.5% lower margins, and 57.4% may be forced to raise prices. MRCA cites raw material shortages from the West Asia war.

evidence.source: The Edge Malaysia on the same SMEAM/MRCA survey
evidence.what_it_says: 73.3% of respondents employ 50 or fewer workers. MRCA cites 'higher operating costs arising from the expanded sales and service tax'.

evidence.source: NST on an SME Association of Malaysia survey
evidence.what_it_says: 83.3% of SMEs reported operating cost increases above 10%, and 63.7% above 30%.
76% said rising fuel prices 'had severely impacted their operations'. More than 80% saw double-digit cost increases. 45% feared serious cash-flow problems.

evidence.source: CPA Australia Small Business Survey 2024-25, Malaysia
evidence.what_it_says: 47.4% said increasing costs had a major negative impact. 'The most burdensome expenses were materials, utility costs, rent, and taxes.'

evidence.source: UOB Business Outlook Study 2025 Malaysia (535 SMEs)
evidence.what_it_says: 50% expect raw material and production costs to rise a lot after US tariffs. Rising operational and manpower costs are listed. The item-to-percentage mapping in the extracted text is uncertain.
After the SST expansion: higher costs for 79.5%, reduced margins for 67.8%, and a heavier admin burden for nearly 50%.

Mustard greens went from RM2.50-3 to RM6-7/kg in two months, and water spinach from about RM3 to about RM18/kg. Members buy only one or two days of stock. 'Customers rarely feel the impact because we cushion it.'
Raw ingredients up 10-20% since the start of the year. Supplies now carry 6% or 8% SST. Holding prices 'is no longer possible.'
Presma: operators face 10-30% cost increases. KPDN warned against unjustified price rises under the Anti-Profiteering Act.
KPDN Johor: 123 cases and RM13,300 in compounds during the Raya 2025 scheme. Most frequent offence: missing price tag. Not eatery-specific.
Cafe and restaurant sales fell 4.6% in Q1 2026 year on year. Restaurants are shrinking portions.

evidence.source: The Sun via Newswav (search summary only)
evidence.what_it_says: An association says 30-35% of new F&B ventures shut within 12-18 months, citing limited pricing power and poor capital planning. Observation, not a survey.

super_pain_test.money: pass: broad, quantified cost rises and margin compression in 2025-2026 surveys
super_pain_test.already_spending: partial: cost-cutting and owner time; no evidence of paid costing tools
super_pain_test.deadline_or_penalty: partial: no hard deadline; price-display compounds and anti-profiteering risk; spoilage from over-buying
super_pain_test.frequency: pass: supplier prices change weekly or daily in F&B

candidates.scope_flags: Not HR. Pricing suggestions are commercial decisions, not financial advice, but keep the owner as decision-maker. Mostly a micro/small problem in F&B. Generic risk: 'rising costs' alone is the 'SMEs are struggling' framing the rubric penalises, so the pitch must be a concrete per-item cost-to-price check. The owners' visibility gap is inferred, not measured.
candidates.why_ranked_here: Deepest survey evidence of any money pain, very current (Oct 2026), with strong F&B owner voice. Product journey: a supplier price change arrives (invoice photo or WhatsApp price list), then recipe and BOM cost per item is recomputed, then rules flag items below the target margin and propose a new price, then the owner approves, then the price list and menu update with a change log ready for price-display compliance. Ranked below P1-P3 because the deadline is soft, there is no evidence of current spend on a fix, and the core visibility gap is inferred.

candidates.title: Construction subcontractors: progress claims paid late ('pay-when-paid') and retention money stuck, with recovery bound to CIPAA's working-day deadlines
candidates.description: Small contractors and subcontractors (M&E, renovation, specialist trades) bill progress claims and get paid late or not at all. Causes include clients withholding payment and 'pay-when-paid' terms. CIPAA 2012 adjudication works only through strict written steps. These include a payment claim with prescribed content and a 10-working-day response window (no response means the whole claim is deemed disputed). Then come 10- and 5-working-day submissions and a 45-working-day decision. A firm that lacks documents (variation orders, delivery records, WhatsApp instructions) loses leverage. Retention of 5-10% per contract is released at completion and after the defects period. Release dates must be tracked per project, and the money is usually lost if the main contractor fails, because it is not trust money unless the contract says so. AIAC CIPAA registrations rose from 29 (2014) to 626 (2024). SMEs are about 70% of the construction sector.
candidates.who: Micro and small contractors and subcontractors (M&E, renovation, specialist trades).
candidates.frequency: Every progress claim on every project, plus two retention-release milestones per project. A monthly claim cadence is typical practice but is not stated in the sources.
candidates.money_impact: Retention is 'typically 5% to 10% of a contract's value', 'often equivalent to several months of operating cash flow' (MCMEA, Jan 2026). Late payment 'causes severe cash flow problems' and 'some companies have to close down' (Planning Malaysia 2020, n=37). Construction delays went from 87 days to 76 days in 2024 (Experian PDF, search excerpt only).
candidates.deadline_or_penalty: CIPAA: payment response in 10 working days; submissions in 10 and 5 working days; decision in 45 working days. Under s.29, a winner may suspend or slow work after 14 days unpaid plus 14 days' notice. Retention is lost on main-contractor insolvency.
candidates.already_spending: Pass. AIAC adjudicator fees: RM3,036 for disputes of RM50,000 and below, RM6,336 for RM50,001-150,000 (excluding taxes). Lawyers and claims consultants. Associations lobbying for retention reform.

evidence.source: SCC Online on the AIAC Asia ADR Week 2026 panel
evidence.what_it_says: 'when CIPAA came into effect in 2014, AIAC recorded 29 cases. By 2024, the number had increased to 626.' Enforcement hurdles described qualitatively.

Payment response within 10 working days, otherwise the party 'is deemed to have disputed the entire payment claim'. Submissions in 10, 10 and 5 working days. Decision 'within 45 working days'. s.29 suspension rights.
RM3,036 for '50,000 and below'. RM6,336 for '50,001 to 150,000'. RM7,796 plus 2.7% of the excess for '150,001 to 300,000'. Excludes taxes.

evidence.source: Planning Malaysia Journal (survey of 37 contractors, Gombak)
evidence.what_it_says: Causes: the client withholding payment and 'pay when paid'. Effects: 'severe cash flow problems to subcontractor(s)'; 'some companies have to close down their services'. Small sample.

evidence.source: Malaysia SME, report of an MCMEA seminar
evidence.what_it_says: SMEs are 'an estimated 70% of Malaysia's construction sector'. Retention is 'typically 5% to 10%', 'often equivalent to several months of operating cash flow'. CIPAA 'does not protect retention sums when insolvency occurs'.
Retention is trust money only with clear contractual language and a separate trust account.

evidence.source: Experian State of Credit 2025 PDF (search excerpt only)
evidence.what_it_says: Construction 'Delays decreased from 87 days in Q1 2024 to 76 days by the end of the year.' Not verified in the PDF body.

super_pain_test.money: pass: retention worth months of cash; documented closures
super_pain_test.already_spending: pass: AIAC fees, lawyers and claims consultants
super_pain_test.deadline_or_penalty: pass: statutory CIPAA working-day windows; deemed dispute if a response is missed
super_pain_test.frequency: partial: per progress claim (monthly typical but unsourced) plus retention milestones

candidates.scope_flags: Close to legal advice: CIPAA notices are legal process. The product must stay preparatory: assemble the evidence pack, track statutory clocks, and remind people about release dates. It must not tell users whether to adjudicate. Vertical niche: reusable across many subcontractors, but less broad for an Orbyte-wide pitch. Some key sources are older (2020, 2022), and the large-project loss examples are not micro.
candidates.why_ranked_here: The highest raw super-pain score: three passes and one partial, with hard statutory clocks and real spend. Clean journey: a claim period ends, then VOs, delivery records and site WhatsApp instructions are gathered against the contract, then completeness rules check the claim and the 10-working-day clock starts, then the owner approves submission, then status is tracked and retention-release reminders are logged. Ranked mid-table because it is one vertical, the evidence is smaller and partly older, and the legal-adjacency risk is higher.

candidates.title: Exempt micro and small suppliers are pressed by big buyers for e-invoices and TINs, and payment is delayed
candidates.description: Since 1 Sep 2026, firms under RM3 million turnover are exempt from MyInvois e-invoicing (verified on the official LHDN/HASiL timeline page, updated 30 Aug 2026). That covers essentially all micro firms and most small services firms. But SME associations report that large, e-invoice-ready customers still ask exempt suppliers for TIN, SSM and SST details and e-invoices. Payment is delayed 'simply because they are not issuing e-invoices'. LHDN says normal receipts remain valid proof of expense, so the pressure comes from buyer confusion, not law. Exemption is not automatic: a group test brings small firms with RM3m+ shareholders or related companies into scope, so status must be re-checked every year. Firms that prepared early have sunk costs. Note: one agent cited only RM500k as officially confirmed, but the compliance and landscape agents verified RM3m on the official LHDN page. Use RM3m. This could also be built as a module of P1.
candidates.who: Micro and small B2B suppliers under RM3m turnover selling to medium or large e-invoicing companies: trading, contractors, services, logistics, F&B suppliers.
candidates.frequency: Every B2B invoice to an affected large customer: weekly or more for active suppliers. The group-test status check is annual.
candidates.money_impact: Payments delayed or withheld. No source gives a ringgit amount. In-scope compliance cost was estimated at up to RM200,000 in year one (Samenta, 2024; an association estimate, not for exempt firms).
candidates.deadline_or_penalty: For exempt firms: commercial only (payment held, risk of exclusion from supply chains). For group-test and RM3m+ firms: RM200-RM20,000 per offence under s120(1)(d) ITA after relaxation ends 31 Dec 2027 (secondary sources).
candidates.already_spending: Pass. Firms 'already incurring' costs on accounting systems and integration before being exempted (The Star, Sep 2026). 57% turn to accountants or advisors on e-invoicing (Xero 2025). One owner: 'Lucky I can cancel my e-invoice subscription'.

evidence.what_it_says: Chin warns of exempt SMEs' 'payments being delayed simply because they are not issuing e-invoices'. Ng: larger clients 'were actively asking some exempt suppliers for information such as their Tax Identification Number'; 'payments should not be withheld'. Koh: some 'may now find themselves exempt after already incurring these costs'.

evidence.source: Malay Mail (SMEAM). Body retrieved by one agent via curl; another saw 403. Dateline given as 17 or 19 Sep.
evidence.what_it_says: Larger e-invoicing companies 'may impose additional layer of requirements for the exempted micro-businesses that could result in payment delays'. 'Even a relatively short delay in receiving payment can create pressure, especially for micro and small businesses'. More than 1.1 million businesses exempt.
'Taxpayers with an annual turnover or revenue of less than RM3,000,000 are exempted from e-Invoice implementation.'
Threshold raised from RM1 million to RM3 million effective 1 Sep 2026. Buyers are affected because suppliers below the threshold may issue non-electronic invoices.
Carve-outs for shareholders, holding and related companies at RM3m+. Relaxation to 31 Dec 2027. 'Your normal receipts remain valid proof of expense for buyers.'
The exemption does not apply where a non-individual shareholder, holding company, related company or JV partner has revenue of RM3m or more.
LHDN: taxpayers can claim deductions using existing documentation such as a normal bill, receipt or invoice.

evidence.source: theSun on the DARE survey (search summary only)
evidence.what_it_says: 516 micro online sellers: 59.9% had never heard of e-invoicing. Ng says large corporations warned non-compliant SME suppliers of exclusion from supply chains.
'the rules kept being tweaked since day 1 until now'. 'Lucky I can cancel my e-invoice subscription'. 'Rip those sudah invest in system kek'.

super_pain_test.money: partial: payments delayed or withheld, but no ringgit figure; evidence is association statements
super_pain_test.already_spending: pass: sunk spend on e-invoice systems and advisors
super_pain_test.deadline_or_penalty: partial: commercial withholding for exempt firms; statutory penalties only for group-test or RM3m+ firms after 2027
super_pain_test.frequency: pass: every invoice to an affected large buyer

candidates.scope_flags: Close to tax advice. The product must quote the LHDN guideline and collect facts. It must not rule on a firm's status as advice, and it must not submit to MyInvois (a statutory filing). Direct proof of withholding rests on two association leaders in one or two articles. Rules have shifted four times, so the pain may fade. Also a natural sub-feature of P1.
candidates.why_ranked_here: Very current (Sep-Oct 2026) and specific to the target users, with sunk spend. A tidy journey: a buyer requests an e-invoice or TIN, then the supplier profile, turnover and group test are pulled together, then rules decide whether an exempt-status pack applies, then the owner approves sending it, then it is sent and the overdue invoice is linked to P1 follow-up and logged. Ranked mid because the withholding evidence is thin and unquantified, and the policy could shift again.

candidates.title: Overlapping statutory deadlines (SST, SSM, stamp duty, council licences, e-invoice Phase 4) run by owners with one or two admin staff
candidates.description: A small firm faces many agency calendars, each with its own portal and penalty. SST-02 returns are due bi-monthly, with nil returns mandatory and late penalties reported to escalate to 40%. Rental service tax is 6% from 2026, and SME tenants must register on MyPMK to get the exemption. SSM annual returns are due within 30 days of the incorporation anniversary, and financial statements within 6+1 months; normal compounds run RM5,000-RM40,000 per offence. Stamp duty self-assessment requires tenancy and lease instruments to be stamped within 30 days from 1 Jan 2026. Council business and signboard licences renew yearly, and DBKL's multi-year renewal is blocked by outstanding compounds. E-invoice Phase 4 firms (RM3m-RM5m turnover, or caught by the group test) must consolidate monthly within 7 days of month-end, and any transaction above RM10,000 needs its own e-invoice. Samenta says compliance costs have reached 'a breaking point' and that small firms lack departments to manage 'overlapping regulatory timelines'. Rules keep changing, and online guides go stale: a Sep 2026 calendar still cites the RM1m e-invoice exemption. SSM's 2026 compound-reduction campaign (90-98.75% off) suggests a sizeable backlog, but no defaulter count was found.
candidates.who: Owners and lean admin staff of micro and small Sdn Bhd firms with physical premises. SST-registrable service providers near the RM500k/RM1m/RM1.5m thresholds. SME tenants of commercial premises. E-invoice Phase 4 applies only to RM3m-RM5m and group-test firms, mostly upper-small.
candidates.frequency: Monthly (e-invoice consolidation for Phase 4), bi-monthly (SST), per agreement (stamp duty), and annual (SSM, licences, Form C). Continuous for the business overall.
candidates.money_impact: SSM compounds RM5,000-RM40,000 per offence, and conviction up to RM50,000 for the company and each officer. SST late penalties up to 40% of tax due (secondary). E-invoice RM200-RM20,000 per offence (secondary). Stamp duty late penalty RM50/10% to RM100/20%, and failing to file up to RM10,000. Samenta: compliance erodes net margins of 10-15%.
candidates.deadline_or_penalty: Hard statutory dates: 30 days (SSM annual return, stamp duty), 7 days after month-end (Phase 4 consolidation), last day of the following month (SST). Licence non-renewal means the premises cannot legally operate.
candidates.already_spending: Pass. Accountants, tax agents and company secretaries (fees not found in these sources). IDEAS 2019: many regulatory payments are 'outsourced'.

evidence.what_it_says: 'the cumulative cost of regulatory compliance reaches a breaking point'. Lists stamp duty self-assessment, BMW toilets, e-invoicing, DPOs and more. Small firms lack departments 'needed to manage these overlapping regulatory timelines'. Net margins 10-15%.
'about 77 per cent are micro businesses', many with 'only one or two administrative staff'. Cites SST thresholds of RM1.5m and RM500k. Asks for 'less frequent reporting'.
Campaign ran 16 Apr-30 Sep 2026. Normal to reduced compounds: s68 annual return RM5,000 to RM500; s248 financial statements RM40,000 to RM500; s245 accounting records RM40,000 to RM2,000.

Annual return due '30 days from the incorporation anniversary'. Confusing it with financial year end is the 'most common filing mistake'. Directors discover overdue filings when a bank or tender committee asks.
Form C within seven months of year end. SST 'six filing cycles a year'. Still describes sub-RM1m firms as exempt from e-invoicing, which is outdated after 1 Sep 2026.
Compound reductions of 90-98.75%, saving 'RM900 and RM39,500 per offence'.

Stamp duty self-assessment Phase 1 from 1 Jan 2026 for rentals and leases. Stamp 'within 30 days'. Late penalty 'RM50 or 10%' then 'RM100 or 20%'. Not filing a return: fine up to RM10,000. Keep records 7 years.
From 1 July 2025 the rental/leasing threshold rises from RM500,000 to RM1 million at 8%.
Rental tax 8% to end-2025, 6% from 1 Jan 2026. Recovered utility charges are taxable. SME tenants must 'Register through the MyPMK System' for the exemption.
SST returns are due every two months by the last day of the following month. Nil returns are mandatory. Late penalties escalate to a 40% cap (secondary).
Strata and pest-control members were paying 'under protest' amid confusing guidelines.
DBKL allows renewal for up to 3 years from 1 July, only with no 'kompaun atau tunggakan bayaran sewa'. About 95,000 licensees.
DBKL issued 211 offence notices for advertisements without a valid licence between Jan and 16 Oct 2024.

Consolidated e-invoices 'must reach MyInvois within 7 calendar days after the end of the month'. The RM10,000 single-transaction rule is not suspended. RM200-RM20,000 and/or 6 months per offence. 'Treat "exempt today" as a status to re-check each year'.
Consolidation is not allowed once a single transaction reaches RM10,000. ACCCIM asks for SME-friendly e-invoicing.

evidence.source: IDEAS (120 micro and small service firms; dated 2019)
evidence.what_it_says: Corporate tax compliance took '44 days of staff time'. Billboard regulation is among the costliest rules. Most payments are over the counter or outsourced.

super_pain_test.money: pass: compounds of RM5,000-RM40,000 per SSM offence, SST penalties up to 40%, licence non-renewal
super_pain_test.already_spending: pass: accountants, tax agents and company secretaries
super_pain_test.frequency: partial: monthly only for Phase 4 firms; otherwise bi-monthly, per agreement or annual

candidates.scope_flags: Submitting statutory filings is OUT of scope, so it must stay a preparatory calendar, readiness checklist and document pack. Close to tax and legal advice on status questions. Risk of being read as 'administrative' work that overlaps Orbyte admin. Orbyte has no compliance module per the landscape agent, but judges may see it as admin. Crowded with accountants and company secretaries who already provide this. Many penalty figures come from secondary advisory sources, not RMCD, LHDN or SSM primary documents. E-invoice Phase 4 mainly hits upper-small firms.
candidates.why_ranked_here: Hard deadlines, real penalties and existing paid help, with many sources. It is reusable across many SMEs as a 'deadline engine' block. Ranked mid-low because the product can only prepare, not file. Weekly frequency is weak for most micro firms. It risks reading as admin. Accountants already own much of this.

candidates.title: Back-office books stay manual, so owners pay accountants to rebuild them and cannot show lenders a financial history
candidates.description: Micro and small firms digitised the front office (WhatsApp, e-wallets) but kept invoicing, bookkeeping and finance tracking on paper, hand-typed invoices and unconnected spreadsheets. KRI/MDEC (May 2026) says micro firms 'frequently rely on informal bookkeeping methods or commingle personal and business accounts'. It says this restricts their ability to apply for financing and grants. BNM names 'thin-file' SMEs (micro, start-ups, informal) as facing financing difficulty. Owners pay outside accountants monthly. Hiring a clerk is hard, so the owner does paperwork after hours. The money cost is accountant fees plus missing cheap facilities (SRF at up to 3.75% p.a.; MSME Digital Grant MADANI at 50% matching up to RM5,000) exactly when cash is tight. The 'manual back office' mechanism item is merged in here.
candidates.who: Micro enterprises (70.1% of MSMEs in 2024), especially owner-run, family-run, home-based or informal firms without separate business accounts. Small owners who outsource bookkeeping.
candidates.frequency: Daily or weekly recording. Monthly accountant cycle. Financing and grant applications are episodic.
candidates.money_impact: Accountant fees: RM500-RM2,000/month (vendor quote). One JB workshop with RM200k revenue pays RM1,500/month (owner voice). Missed or costlier financing is not quantified. Only 36.7% found external finance easy to access (CPA Australia 2024).
candidates.deadline_or_penalty: Weak. Missed financing or grant windows. Annual tax filing (rule not verified in these sources). No direct regulatory penalty for informal books was found for micro firms.
candidates.already_spending: Pass. Outsourced accountants, bookkeepers and tax agents. 57% consult accountants or advisors on e-invoicing (Xero 2025).

evidence.source: KRI and MDEC discussion paper 'From Survival to Scale'
evidence.what_it_says: 'Micro-enterprises, in particular, frequently rely on informal bookkeeping methods or commingle personal and business accounts'. 'poor bookkeeping practices, incomplete documentation, and reliance on personal bank accounts ... restrict their ability to apply for financing'. Micro firms are 70.1% of MSMEs. Back-end processes 'remain manual and disconnected'.
Customer-facing functions are digitised while back-end processes stay manual. 'limited documentation, weak record-keeping'.

evidence.source: The Star interview with BNM Assistant Governor
evidence.what_it_says: Thin-file SMEs 'typically lack a track record, formal financial history, or sufficient collateral', including microenterprises and informal businesses.

evidence.source: Xero whitepaper (500 SMEs, Apr-May 2025; vendor survey)
evidence.what_it_says: 32% still rely on manual invoicing. 57% turn to accountants, bookkeepers or advisors. Expected benefits named: improved recordkeeping 72%.
'accounting services are also costing him an extra RM 1,500 per month!' Handwritten bills for 20 years. 'Nowadays, hiring a clerk is difficult'. 'The biggest issue is time.'
'it started feeling more like a full-time job'. 'Better to hire an accountant. No way around it.' 'The more manual work involved, the higher the risk of errors.'
Bookkeeping services 'usually start from RM500 and may go up to RM1,500 or RM2,000 per month'.
Only 46% of MSMEs use online solutions for finance and accounting.
Insufficient documentation is cited as the top reason SME loan applications are rejected.

super_pain_test.money: partial: accountant fees evidenced; cost of lost financing not quantified
super_pain_test.deadline_or_penalty: fail/partial: no hard deadline; financing windows are episodic
super_pain_test.frequency: pass: daily recording and monthly accountant cycle

candidates.scope_flags: It must not give financial advice or make lending decisions. A 'lender-ready pack' must stay preparatory. Crowded: accounting tools exist (Bukku free tier, SQL, AutoCount, Financio) and Orbyte plans accounting partners via Connect, so the team must not rebuild accounting software. Receipt capture resembles Orbyte eClaim (an HR expense module), so avoid that overlap. Risk of the generic 'SMEs are disorganised' framing.
candidates.why_ranked_here: Well evidenced as a root cause (KRI/MDEC, BNM), with clear existing spend. But it has no deadline, and its money link is indirect. It overlaps accounting tools and Orbyte's partner plans. Best used as the data foundation under P1 or P4, not as the headline pain.

candidates.title: F&B premises compliance: every food handler needs typhoid vaccination and training proof, and licence renewal now depends on toilet standards
candidates.description: Under the Food Hygiene Regulations 2009, every food handler must be typhoid-vaccinated and trained at an MOH-recognised school. MOH warns of closure orders of up to 14 days under s11 Food Act 1983, plus fines. Enforcement is visible every Ramadan: 1,639 notices (RM163,900 in compounds) and 3 closures in 2024, and in Kedah 112 compounds after 3% of handlers were found unvaccinated and 10% untrained. One agent dates the Kedah figures to 2025 (theSun) and another to 2026 (Malay Mail, 1 Mar 2026), so the date is a CONFLICT to resolve. Separately, from January 2026 food premises in 20 city areas will not have business licences renewed if toilets fail the 'BMW' standard, with phasing to municipal (2027) and district councils (2028). The busywork: keeping each worker's proof on file, catching new hires without it, and producing documents at a surprise inspection.
candidates.who: Micro and small F&B operators: restaurants, cafes, stalls, caterers, bazaar and expo vendors. BMW rule: food premises in city council areas first.
candidates.frequency: Every new hire, plus surprise inspections with Ramadan enforcement peaks. Annual licence renewal. Typhoid validity period was NOT verified.
candidates.money_impact: Closure of up to 14 days means about two weeks of lost revenue. Compounds are roughly RM100-RM125 each on average (RM163,900 across 1,639 notices in 2024; RM14,000 across 112 in Kedah). Toilet upgrade costs are not quantified.
candidates.deadline_or_penalty: Closure orders (s11 Food Act), compounds and fines. Licence non-renewal for BMW failures.
candidates.already_spending: Unknown. The vaccine is reportedly free at government clinics. Training course costs were not found.

evidence.what_it_says: Every food handler must be typhoid-vaccinated and trained at MOH-recognised schools. Closure orders of up to 14 days under s11 Food Act 1983, plus fines.
1,639 notices under s32B at 2024 Ramadan bazaars. 3 premises ordered closed.

evidence.source: Malay Mail AMP version of the same article (search summary)
evidence.what_it_says: Compound values of RM163,900, covering failures such as no food-handler training or no typhoid vaccination.
Kedah: 112 compounds worth RM14,000 at 80 bazaar sites. 3% of handlers unvaccinated and 10% untrained.

evidence.date: 2025 (per agent; conflicts with the Malay Mail 2026 date)
evidence.what_it_says: The same Kedah figures: 112 compounds, 3% unvaccinated, 10% untrained.
From January 2026, food premises in 20 city areas 'will not have their business licences renewed if they fail to meet the BMW level'.
City councils in 2026, municipal councils in 2027, district councils in 2028.

super_pain_test.money: partial: closure means lost revenue, but compounds are small
super_pain_test.deadline_or_penalty: pass: closure orders and licence non-renewal
super_pain_test.frequency: partial: per hire and per inspection; licences annual

candidates.scope_flags: HR overlap risk: per-staff vaccination and training records sit close to Orbyte People/Directory. Frame it as premises compliance readiness, not staff records. F&B only. Most evidence is search summaries from Malay Mail and theSun (403), and the Kedah date conflicts. Health data on staff raises PDPA sensitivity.
candidates.why_ranked_here: Real, enforced penalties for the exact target users, but the money is modest and spend is unknown. Evidence is mostly unfetched snippets. It also sits near Orbyte's HR modules. Better as a roadmap extension of P7 than as the headline.

candidates.title: Platform fee creep (Shopee, TikTok Shop, delivery apps) eats margins, and sellers cannot see true profit per order
candidates.description: Marketplace and delivery fees take a large, shifting share of each order, changing on different dates. Shopee: transaction fee from 2% to 3.5% (Aug 2024), SPayLater seller fee from 3.5% to 4.5% (May 2025), a RM0.50 per-order fee from July 2025, and commission changes in Feb and May 2026. Sources CONFLICT on whether its 5% technical support fee applies to local sellers. TikTok Shop: RM0.50 (RM0.54 with SST) platform support fee per delivered order from 15 Feb 2026, charged even if the order is later refunded, plus higher category commissions from 31 Oct 2026. Food delivery: Samenta (2024) says up to 32% commission, and up to 60% with promotions. Vendors put 2026 rates at 12-22%. Merchants mark up 30-100% on apps or push regulars to WhatsApp ordering, which brings back manual order-taking. Owners struggle to know the real margin per SKU or dish and when to reprice.
candidates.who: Micro and small online sellers on Shopee and TikTok Shop selling low-value goods. Micro F&B outlets and hawkers on GrabFood, foodpanda and ShopeeFood.
candidates.frequency: Every order, daily. Fee rules changed several times a year (Aug 2024, May 2025, Jul 2025, Feb 2026, May 2026, Oct 2026).
candidates.money_impact: Delivery commission up to 32%, or up to 60% with promotions (Samenta 2024). Vendor estimates for 2026: 15-22% (GrabFood). TikTok Shop about 14-19% plus RM0.54 per order (vendor). Sellers say the RM0.50 Shopee fee alone 'is more than our profit' on low-value orders.
candidates.deadline_or_penalty: No fine. Fees take effect on fixed dates, and sellers who do not reprice lose margin on every order from that date.
candidates.already_spending: Pass. The fees themselves, plus ERP and fee-calculator tools (BigSeller, Inseller).

evidence.what_it_says: SPayLater seller fee rises from 3.5% to 4.5% from 8 May 2025, with no opt-out. The transaction fee had already risen from 2% to 3.5% in Aug 2024. Sellers plan to raise prices or move away from Shopee.
Platform Support Fee of RM0.50 excluding SST (RM0.54 with SST) per delivered order, still charged if the order is later returned or refunded.
TikTok Shop raises most category commissions from 31 Oct 2026. Example: non-BXP Mall beauty from 18.90% to 20.52%.
Opposes a 2-3% commission rise and a RM0.50 per-order fee from 16 July 2025. 'the RM0.50 fee alone is more than our profit.'
RM13.64 deducted on a RM100 electronics order, including a 5% technical support fee it says applies to all sellers. Commission rose on 1 Feb and 21 May 2026.
CONTRADICTS Jumix: the 5% fee applies to cross-border sellers only.
A programme seller pays about 18.9% of order value plus RM0.54 per order. Outside the programme, about 14% plus RM0.54.
Merchants are charged 'up to 32 per cent commission on every delivery', and up to 60% with promotions and marketing fees.

evidence.source: Borneo Post (same Samenta statement; search result)
evidence.what_it_says: Merchants mark up app prices by 30 to 100% to stay marginally profitable.
GrabFood 15-22%, foodpanda 12-20%, ShopeeFood 10-18%. RM10,800 a month on RM60,000 GMV at 18%.

super_pain_test.money: pass: double-digit share of every order
super_pain_test.already_spending: pass: fees paid automatically; ERP tools bought
super_pain_test.deadline_or_penalty: partial: fixed effective dates, but no penalty

candidates.scope_flags: A product cannot remove the fees. It can only reveal true margin and trigger repricing or a channel shift, which overlaps P4's logic (consider merging into P4 as one 'true margin' engine). Crowded with seller ERPs (BigSeller and others). Recent commission figures are vendor-sourced, and the 5% fee question is unresolved. Not HR.
candidates.why_ranked_here: Passes money, spend and frequency with official fee pages. But the burden is structural, not an operational task the product can remove, and existing ERPs already compete. Strongest as an extra cost input to P4.

candidates.title: GP and panel clinics: third-party administrator (TPA) reimbursements take months, with deductions and onboarding fees
candidates.description: Small private GP clinics treat corporate panel patients, then claim from TPAs. Doctors' associations (Nov 2025) report payment cycles 'stretching for months'. They also report part-payments, 'adjustments and discrepancy deductions', TPAs taking as much as 10% of GP fees per visit, and panel onboarding fees of up to RM5,000. Clinics reconcile claims against payments across several TPAs by hand. They lose everything if a TPA collapses: one doctor had RM24,000 unpaid after two TPAs failed (2019), and a TPA owed doctors more than RM1 million (2014). Associations say the problem has run for nearly 20 years. This is a vertical form of the receivables pain in P1, with an added reconciliation step.
candidates.who: Micro and small private GP clinics (owner-doctor plus a few staff).
candidates.frequency: A claim on every panel visit, daily. Reconciliation and chasing happen per TPA cycle, monthly or longer.
candidates.money_impact: Up to 10% of GP fees per visit deducted. Onboarding fees of up to RM5,000. Months of cash tied up. Total-loss risk shown by RM24,000 (2019) and more than RM1m (2014) cases.
candidates.deadline_or_penalty: No statutory deadline on TPAs was found. Forced consequence: cash tied up, plus total loss if a TPA collapses.
candidates.already_spending: Pass. Onboarding and panel fees, per-patient deductions, and staff time on claims (not quantified).

evidence.what_it_says: 'chronic delays in reimbursement to clinics, with payment cycles stretching for months'. Clinics are treated as 'unpaid financiers of TPA operations'. Onboarding fees 'as high as RM5,000'. Nearly two decades of concerns.

evidence.source: CodeBlue op-ed (Association of Private Practitioners Sabah founder)
evidence.what_it_says: 'slicing off as much as 10 per cent of GP total fees per patient visit'. Months to reimburse. Incomplete payment through 'adjustments and discrepancy deductions'.
TPAs charge RM2-RM5 per patient as a panel fee and set consultation fees at RM10-RM15. Staged part-payments. One doctor had RM24,000 unpaid.
A TPA owed doctors more than RM1 million. One doctor was still owed RM15,657 for services in 2011-2012.

super_pain_test.money: pass: months of delay, 10% deductions, total-loss cases
super_pain_test.already_spending: pass: onboarding fees of up to RM5,000 and per-visit deductions
super_pain_test.deadline_or_penalty: partial: no statutory deadline; cash squeeze and collapse risk
super_pain_test.frequency: pass: daily claims and monthly reconciliation

candidates.scope_flags: Healthcare vertical: patient data is sensitive under PDPA (synthetic data only). Narrow segment for an Orbyte-wide pitch. Medical billing rules are specialised. The current evidence comes from association statements and an op-ed, not surveys.
candidates.why_ranked_here: A strong, specific super-pain with recent association evidence, a clear journey (TPA remittance arrives, then match against submitted claims, then flag short-paid or overdue items, then clinic manager approves the dispute or chase, then sent and logged), and it reuses P1 logic. Ranked low because the evidence base is small (two CodeBlue pieces plus older reports), it is a single vertical, and patient data is sensitive.

candidates.title: Marketplace shipping deadlines and penalty points: late shipment, overselling cancellations and refund windows
candidates.description: Shopee scores sellers on a rolling 7-day Late Shipment Rate. Since 8 Apr 2026 the threshold is 10% for regular sellers and 5% for Mall/Preferred. A breach adds penalty points that can suspend seller privileges for up to 28 days. Fast Handover Rate joined the penalty system from 11 May 2026 (snippet). Shopee, Lazada and TikTok Shop have no native cross-platform stock sync, so selling the same unit on two channels causes cancellations that count against the seller. TikTok Shop reportedly auto-approves refunds after 48 hours without a response (unverified). Vendors name 'disorganised inventory, missed cut-off times, and no clear order-monitoring process' as causes. Sellers who also take WhatsApp orders juggle stock by hand.
candidates.who: Micro and small multi-channel online sellers (Shopee, TikTok Shop, Lazada), often also selling on WhatsApp.
candidates.frequency: Daily shipping cut-offs. Metrics recalculated on a rolling 7 days.
candidates.money_impact: Not quantified. Up to 28 days of suspended privileges, loss of visibility or campaign eligibility, and Mall/Preferred offboarding. Auto-approved refunds lose both goods and payment.
candidates.deadline_or_penalty: Hard ship-by deadlines and penalty points escalating to suspension. A 48-hour refund response window on TikTok (unverified).
candidates.already_spending: Partial. Some sellers buy ERP/OMS tools such as BigSeller. Spend level unknown.

evidence.what_it_says: LSR thresholds 10% regular and 5% Mall/Preferred from 8 Apr 2026. 1 or 2 penalty points per breach. 'suspension of seller privileges for up to 28 days'. Causes include 'disorganised inventory, missed cut-off times, and no clear order-monitoring process'.
Fast Handover Rate joins Seller Penalty Points from 11 May 2026. Non-fulfilment rate should stay below 10%.
There is no native cross-platform stock sync. Cancellations from overselling count toward cancellation-rate thresholds.
Tiered penalties from warning to reduced visibility up to store suspension or closure.
TikTok Shop refund requests not handled within 48 hours are auto-approved.
Micro-sellers on WhatsApp and Instagram DMs lose orders in chat history or copy them into Excel by hand.

super_pain_test.money: partial: suspension and visibility loss are real but unquantified
super_pain_test.already_spending: partial: ERP and OMS tools bought; spend unknown
super_pain_test.deadline_or_penalty: pass: hard ship-by deadlines and escalating penalty points

candidates.scope_flags: Evidence is almost entirely from one seller-ERP vendor (BigSeller) plus unverified snippets, with no official Shopee or TikTok policy page fetched for penalties. A crowded market of multichannel ERPs. Real deployment needs marketplace API integration (simulated in the hackathon). Not HR.
candidates.why_ranked_here: Hard deadlines and a daily rhythm suit an automated trigger (a 'ship-by in 4h, stock conflict detected' alert, then owner approval of cancel or reallocate). But the money impact is unquantified, the sources are vendor-only, and incumbents already sell this. Last place.

dropped.title: Thin cash buffers / no forward cash view (standalone)
dropped.reason: Merged into P1 as its consequence. On its own it is a state, not a recurring task a product can remove. Survey figures also conflict (Samenta 70% under 6 months vs SME Bank 70% over 6 months).

dropped.title: Back office stays manual and disconnected (mechanism)
dropped.reason: The surveys agent itself framed this as the root mechanism, not a super pain. Merged into P8. As a standalone it is the generic 'SMEs are inefficient' framing the rubric penalises, and 'connect everything' overlaps Orbyte Connect.

dropped.title: Available tools are costly, fragmented and shallowly adopted; grant payouts slow
dropped.reason: A structural barrier, not a recurring burden. A 'one hub for disconnected tools' idea duplicates Orbyte's own core pitch and Connect module.

dropped.title: Payroll and minimum-wage compliance (RM1,700, possibly RM2,000 from June 2027)
dropped.reason: HR/payroll overlaps Orbyte People and its stated payroll partners. Budget 2027 reportedly exempts MSMEs under RM50m sales from the next wage rise (search-level, unverified).

dropped.title: Monthly EPF/SOCSO deadlines and enforcement
dropped.reason: HR/payroll overlap. Enforcement data (from a 403'd theSun snippet) is not split by firm size or cause. Low confidence.

dropped.reason: Software cannot supply workers. This is HR. Evidence is a single industry-group claim.

merged_candidates.orbyte_profile:
Source: the landscape agent read orbyte.my (index, contact, modules, pricing, partners, platform and FAQ pages) on 2026-10-24. Everything here comes from Orbyte's own site, with no independent confirmation.

WHAT IT IS: an 'AI-native operating system' and daily-actions layer for SMEs that 'juggle disconnected tools like messaging apps, email, spreadsheets, HR software and accounting systems'. It explicitly says it is NOT an HRMS, ERP or chatbot. Approved results are written back to the customer's HR or accounting system of record. The walkthrough form offers team sizes 1-20, 21-50, 51-200 and 200+.

LIVE MODULES (do not duplicate):
- People: eLeave, eClaim (AI receipt reading and policy flags), eOT, Attendance, Directory and announcements.
- Work: Daily Work Status and Monthly Project Focus (free).
- Hiring: job post, AI screening and scoring, stage tracking; explicitly 'not a full ATS'.
- eSign: built on Documenso, with audit log.
- Connect: SSO, access control, roles and approval workflows over third-party SaaS and payment services. Categories: payments and collections, financing referral, accounting and payroll, sales and CRM, e-commerce and POS.
- Platform-wide: org structure, review and approval with audit trail, Entra ID, Google and Microsoft sign-in, clients and projects, resource profiles.

COMING SOON: Travel, and Insights (performance trends, described as 'not surveillance scores').

STATED DIRECTION (intent, not shipped): integrated partners for payroll, accounting and e-invoicing, payments and banking, logistics, marketing, insurance, POS and e-commerce. Also an open API, marketplace and developer ecosystem, and a 'Business Graph' linking projects, invoices, payment terms and cash flow. AI examples include 'follow up unpaid invoices'.

NOT BUILT OR MENTIONED: native invoicing, receivables, accounting, e-invoicing, inventory, sales/CRM, WhatsApp, or anything customer-facing. These money-side and WhatsApp-channel workflows are white space. Candidates P1-P6 fall there, and P1 matches the stated roadmap.

PRICING: usage-based, one credit wallet, no per-seat fees. Models: Free, Freemium, Transaction, Premium and Partner. Per-unit charging (per claim, per eOT request, per signed document). NO ringgit amounts are published.

COULD NOT BE VERIFIED:
- The site says Orbyte is 'a product of Alpha Red Pro Sdn Bhd' (KL), not 'Alpha Red Solutions Sdn Bhd', the named hackathon sponsor. Search snippets show Alpha Red Solutions (alphareds.com; CTOS company no. 870545X, incorporated 2009) as travel-tech middleware (GrandeConnect) and fintech (Grande DigiFin). How the two entities relate is unconfirmed (an SSM check is needed).
- No RM prices, named partners or integrations (other than Documenso), launch date, customer count, press coverage, funding or dated roadmap were found.
- A web search returned no external Orbyte coverage.

The other six research agents did not research Orbyte.

reality.reasoning:
Verdict: weakened. The pain is real, recent and Malaysian. It is not a standalone super pain. It fails two of the four bars, and the costly part happens outside anything an in-scope product can touch. It is worth building only as a red-flag layer inside a broader WhatsApp order-intake workflow, not as the lead pitch.

What survives:
- Money and penalty pass. Large losses keep recurring in 2026 despite police publicity:
  - NST, 6 May 2026: 80 cases and RM1.9 million so far in 2026, after 241 cases and over RM8 million in 2025.
  - The Star, 12 Sep 2026: the KL Department of Environment saw 8 cases, with two suppliers losing more than RM200,000.
  - The Vibes, 13 Sep 2026: a Raub printing shop lost RM315,963, which was its business savings.
  - Miri, May 2026: five small flower and gift traders lost more than RM28,000.
  - Terengganu, March 2026: a batik trader lost RM48,300 after a WhatsApp order.
- Free awareness alone is not working, so a structural gate is not pointless.

Attacks that land:
1. Each business is rarely hit. Nationally there were 241 cases in 2025 (about 4-5 a week), spread across a very large number of MSMEs. Perak alone had 66 cases in 2025. I could not verify the national micro-firm count: DOSM returned a database error, SME Corp returned 403, and the session's search budget ran out. For any one firm this is an occasional disaster, like insurance, not a weekly cost. The 'daily order screening' frequency is the frequency of the proposed workflow, not of the pain.
2. Nobody is paying for this today. No source shows owners spending money or staff hours on verification. Free defences already exist:
   - PDRM's Semak Mule checks bank accounts, phone numbers and company names. RinggitPlus (6 Nov 2025) describes it as free.
   - CCID Infoline 013-211 1222, and the 997 NSRC hotline.
   - Phoning or visiting the agency, which is what Miri police advised.
   Semak Mule has a stated limit: 'no match doesn't mean a transaction is safe'. That leaves room for rule-based red flags, but no evidence that anyone would pay for them.
3. The loss happens in the bank app, not in the order. In both pattern (a) MOs the money is lost when the owner prepays a 'supplier' the buyer named. In the Perak cases (Utusan, FMT, SAYS) that supplier is for items the business does not make. In KL DOE it is an 'advance payment'. The hackathon bans processing payments, so the product cannot hold or block that transfer. Its 'approval gate' is only advisory. In a 1-4 person micro firm, the approver is usually the same owner who is being deceived. A gate adds real control only where staff take orders and the owner approves.
4. The deposit rule clashes with real government orders. A Penampang caterer took no deposit because 'This is apparently how government orders work' (MustShareNews, 2023, article's own words). Government buyers pay after delivery, so a 'refused deposit' red flag would fire on every genuine government LO. That rule is weak for pattern (a). The stronger rules are: items outside the catalogue, a third-party supplier named by the buyer, and a request to prepay that supplier.
5. Pattern (b), consumer no-shows and refused deposits, is largely solved already, and the evidence is thin:
   - The evidence is dated (2022-2023) and anecdotal, and the amounts are small (RM300).
   - Sellers already fixed it with a policy, not software. Kosmo (21 Apr 2023) reports a George Town bakery adopting 'booking with payment' and another using instalments ('Habis bayar baru dapat biskut raya').
   - Take App's free Basic plan (50 orders a month) already offers WhatsApp order forms with date and time slots, festive pre-orders, and DuitNow/TNG/bank transfer with payment-proof upload. This is vendor-stated, and its adoption in Malaysia is unverified.
6. Victims are not always micro firms. The NST national figure does not describe victim size. Some victims are B2G suppliers making six-figure transfers: a diving-equipment supplier in KL DOE, and the Raub shop. These are small firms or government vendors rather than home kuih sellers.

Scope: there is no HR overlap. The product must not process payments, and supplier holds can only be simulated. It risks becoming a generic 'scam checker' if it is not anchored to order intake.

Net: keep P2 as a feature, not the headline. Concretely, P2 can supply explainable red-flag rules (out-of-catalogue item, buyer-named supplier, prepay request, government letterhead) plus a Semak Mule lookup prompt, inside a broader WhatsApp order-capture product that solves a frequent pain.
reality.corrected_claims:
1. "Police advice each time is the same manual checklist" is overstated. The FMT/Bernama (17 Mar 2026), SAYS (18 Mar 2026) and NST (6 May 2026) articles contain no specific police advice. The Raub article (13 Sep 2026) gives none either. Advice appears in Utusan (18 Mar 2026: meet in person, 'ambil deposit terlebih dahulu sebelum menyediakan pesanan') and in The Vibes on Miri (24 May 2026: confirm by phone or in person; letterheads can be forged).
2. On the Perak losses, the outlets differ. FMT/Bernama says "over RM300,000", while Utusan and SAYS say "hampir RM300,000" (nearly RM300,000). Quote it as "about RM300,000".
3. The NST national figures (241 cases and over RM8m in 2025; 80 cases and RM1.9m by May 2026) cover souvenir and food orders together. The NST article does not describe victim business type or size, so "victims are clearly micro firms" is supported only by the regional cases, not by the national total.
4. In the Raub case (The Vibes, 13 Sep 2026), the owner asked for the supplier's registration and TIN only AFTER paying. The order arrived by WhatsApp from a fake 'PPD Kuala Kangsar' contact. She paid RM18,498 first, then RM297,465 more after receiving an LO.
5. "Refused deposit" is not a reliable red flag for government-impersonation orders. Real government orders are paid after delivery (MustShareNews, 5 Jun 2023, which says "This is apparently how government orders work"). The losses come from prepaying a buyer-named third-party supplier, not from a missing deposit.
6. Pattern (b) money impact (RM300 doughnuts, a RM5 kuih debt) is small and dated (2022-2023). Sellers report solving it themselves with 'booking with payment' or instalments (Kosmo, 21 Apr 2023).
7. Additional 2026 data: KL DOE reported 8 fake-procurement cases, with more than RM200,000 lost by two suppliers (The Star, 12 Sep 2026). A Terengganu batik trader lost RM48,300 after a WhatsApp order from a fake DOE contact (The Vibes, 10 Mar 2026).

new_evidence.what_it_says: Semak Mule is a free PDRM tool that checks bank account numbers, phone numbers and company names reported for fraud. A match means the details were reported before. No match does not mean a transaction is safe. This is a free partial substitute for verifying suppliers.

A George Town baker said: 'terpaksa menggunakan konsep booking with payment bagi mengelak kerugian berganda'. Another bakery uses instalments: 'Habis bayar baru dapat biskut raya'. Sellers already counter consumer no-shows with a payment-first policy and no tool.

The free Basic plan allows 50 orders a month with local payment methods. It offers WhatsApp checkout with a date and time slot, festive pre-order catalogues, and DuitNow, Touch 'n Go and bank transfer with payment-proof upload. The Business plan is USD 50 a month. Deposits are not mentioned. These are vendor claims, and adoption is unverified.

'eight cases involving fake government procurement orders resulting in losses of more than RM200,000 for two suppliers'. The orders used forged documents, fake letterheads and signatures. Suppliers 'transferred more than RM100,000 to certain parties as an advance payment'. One victim was a diving-equipment supplier.

A 59-year-old Terengganu batik trader lost RM48,300 in three transfers. It started with 'a WhatsApp message from a phone number claiming to represent the Department of Environment'. The buyer ordered 50 batik pairs worth RM9,000, added gift items, and directed her to a bogus supplier.

Seven Perak reports with losses of 'hampir RM300,000', targeting 'pengusaha katering dan pastri'. 66 cases were recorded in the state in 2025. Police advise meeting in person and 'ambil deposit terlebih dahulu sebelum menyediakan pesanan'.

The caterer was not suspicious when the buyer could not pay a deposit; the article says 'This is apparently how government orders work.' A real government buyer refusing a deposit is normal, so a deposit red flag gives false positives on government orders.

evidence.reasoning:
Mostly real. I re-fetched 12 of the 13 URLs; Malay Mail returned 403 twice. Recent Malaysian sources confirm the pattern and the cases are real. Three things make it weaker than claimed: the headline national statistic, two misquotes, and the frequency and spending legs.

1) NST 2026-05-06 (national figure). The numbers are quoted correctly: "241 cases were reported in 2025, with total losses amounting to over RM8 million", and 80 cases / RM1.9 million so far in 2026, per CCID director Rusdi Mohd Isa. The article covers "souvenirs or food". It is ambiguous about who the victims are. The opening line says "a scam syndicate posing as non-existent suppliers". It also says suspects "contact victims as if placing legitimate orders", and that after payment "the goods would never be delivered". It does not say the victims are sellers, micro firms, or businesses at all. It gives no size breakdown and no prevention advice. So "241 such cases hitting micro caterers and sellers" is an inference, not a sourced fact. The 4-5 per week arithmetic is correct (241/52 = 4.6).

2) Perak cluster (FMT English and Malay, both Bernama; RTM). Confirmed: 7 reports from bakeries and caterers. The extra items are "usually ones not produced by the business operator". The scammer refers the victim to another phone number posing as a supplier, takes an upfront payment, then disappears. Discrepancies: FMT says "over RM300,000" but RTM says "hampir RM300,000" (nearly). The English FMT article has no police advice. The Malay FMT article advises "mendapatkan deposit atau membuat pengesahan terlebih dahulu, sebelum menerima tempahan dalam jumlah besar" (get a deposit or verify first, before accepting large orders). RTM advises wariness of unusual orders, dealing face to face, and taking a deposit, so the "manual checklist" claim holds. The claim says "66 cases recorded in Perak". RTM says 66 cases last year and does not clearly say Perak only.

3) Individual cases.
- Raub, The Vibes, 13 Sep 2026: confirmed. RM315,963, "photocopying and printer-related services business", loss "comprised the victim's business savings", fake PPD Kuala Kangsar LO, a supplier phone number, and a request for registration documents and TIN with no reply. Firm size is not stated.
- Kuantan, 25 Sep 2025: confirmed. RM89,300, forged LO and vendor appointment letters, payment to "personal bank accounts", "a consistent modus operandi across the cases". Trader types are not stated; the goods sought were curtains, food, souvenirs and catering.
- Miri, 24 May 2026: confirmed. "FIVE small-scale traders specialising in flowers and gift items", more than RM28,000, mule accounts, and the advice to confirm by phone or in person and not trust letterheads. This is the clearest micro-firm evidence.
- RM175k case, previously unfetched: confirmed at RM175,452.80. KBS was impersonated, and the extra orders were for dates, keris and plaques. When his usual supplier could not fill the order, the suspect referred him to another supplier. The money was his own and his business partner's savings. Published 15 Jun 2025.
- MustShareNews (Penampang, 2023): facts confirmed (150 lunch sets, a supposed army officer, no deposit, then blocked). Misquote: the claim puts "government orders are typically paid only after fulfilment" in quotation marks. The source says "This is apparently how government orders work."
- SAYS (2022) and Kosmo (2023): confirmed, but dated and anecdotal.
- Malay Mail: unverified (403).
- theSun: not re-fetched; the claim had already flagged it as unverified.

4) Scope. The pattern-(b) consumer cancellation evidence is all 2022-2023 anecdote. No source supports "consumer cancellations recur weekly in festive peaks". Fraud hits any one business rarely: 241 national cases a year against a very large micro-firm base. No source shows owners spending on verification; Kosmo shows only a process change to "booking with payment". The claim's own super-pain test is therefore accurate: money and penalty pass, already-spending fails, frequency is partial.

5) Independent source search. My web search budget for the session was used up, so I could not search for a new source. Instead I fetched and verified three cited sources that had not been checked: RTM (previously "search summary only"), the Malay FMT/Bernama version, and The Vibes RM175k article. Browsing the FMT tag pages found no further cases.

Net: the pattern is real, recent, Malaysian and costly per incident, with micro victims clearly shown in Miri, Penampang and the home sellers. The national figure is not specific to micro sellers. There are two quotation errors, and the frequency and spending legs are thin.
