(2) Money kept: 'claimed paid, not received' flags catch deposits that never arrived (synthetic example: RM120). Our hypothesis is 1-3 such cases a month for an active WhatsApp seller; this is unverified. (3) Accountant cost: Mishu (posted 12 Mar 2021, Sdn Bhd) puts outsourced accounting at 'around RM5,000 a year'. One second-hand Lowyat anecdote cites RM1,800/year before e-invoicing. If cleaner hand-offs cut clean-up work by 20-30%, the saving would be roughly RM360-RM1,500/year. That is an estimate, to be validated with 3 accountants. (4) Compliance hygiene: LHDN Public Ruling 5/2000 (Revised) is for sole proprietors and partnerships (issued 30 Jun 2001 and still hosted on hasil.gov.my; we have not verified whether it has been superseded). It says entries should be recorded 'not later than 60 days after the transaction'. It also says that where no separate account is kept, 'a record should be kept to identify the transactions which are for business purposes'. Insufficient records can lead to a best-judgement assessment, an audit at the owner's expense, or a fine of RM300-RM10,000. A weekly lock keeps entries well inside 60 days. (5) Financing path: after 6-12 locked months the owner holds a separated business history. That covers the kind of 'bank statements and transaction records' and 'sales records' the BNM SRF FAQ (Oct 2026) says banks may require, and BNM's Micro Enterprises Facility offers up to RM100,000. We would not claim that approval follows. (6) Demo accuracy target: at least 90% of lines handled correctly on a 300-line labelled synthetic set, with 100% of low-confidence lines routed to a human. SDG 8.3 (formalisation of micro enterprises and their access to finance) and SDG 8.2 (productivity).
ideas.orbyte_fit_and_reuse: It reuses Orbyte's platform: review and approval with an audit trail, roles, and Clients for customer and nickname matching. It reads money data through the Connect 'payments and collections' category and writes the locked ledger back through the 'accounting and payroll' category. This follows Orbyte's stated pattern of writing approved results back to the system of record, so Asing is not a new accounting package. It feeds the stated Business Graph (invoices, payment terms, cash flow). Its 'not received' flags feed Orbyte's stated 'follow up unpaid invoices' AI (P1). Reusable building block: a Transaction Matcher API. Input: transactions plus evidence sources (chats, invoices, POS). Output: class, match, confidence, reason and cited IDs. Sector packs (category templates plus typical patterns) cover home F&B, tailoring, salon, workshop and online reselling. Language packs cover BM, EN and ZH, with Tamil on the roadmap. Bank CSV mapping profiles mean it works with any bank. It is distinct from eClaim: eClaim reimburses employee expenses from receipts, while Asing separates the owner's own commingled account and matches customer payments.
ideas.scope_check: Not HR or admin: no leave, claims, overtime, attendance or payroll. No real payments: money data is read-only and customer messages need approval (simulated in the demo). No statutory filing: it does not file Form B or submit e-invoices. LHDN exempts firms under RM3,000,000 turnover from e-invoicing (timeline updated 30 Aug 2026), so e-invoicing is not used as the pitch hook. No tax, legal or financial advice: categories are bookkeeping labels, and deductibility and split percentages are set by the owner or accountant. No lending decisions. PDPA 2010: the demo uses synthetic data only. In real use: the owner consents to each connector (Notice and Choice). Bank account numbers are masked on import and third-party names are kept only for matching (Disclosure and purpose limitation). Personal lines are visible to the owner only and are excluded from every export. The LLM receives masked, minimal text, and customer data is not used for training. After lock, personal-line descriptions are purged by default, leaving only the amount and a 'personal' tag (Retention). Business records are kept for the 7-year record period. Access is logged (Security and Access principles).
ideas.prelim_demo_scope: One live journey. Load a synthetic week: bank CSV, e-wallet CSV, and a WhatsApp chat JSON in BM, Manglish and Chinese. Rules and the LLM classify and match each line, with reasons. The exception queue shows the bank line and chat bubble side by side, and the owner resolves 3 items with one tap. The owner approves 'Lock Week 43'. The demo then shows the locked ledger, the 'RM120 not received' flag, the activity log, and a CSV export labelled 'accountant view'. The single most important feature is the match-and-explain exception queue that ends in the owner's lock approval. Also show a precision number measured on the labelled synthetic set.
ideas.hardest_risk_and_fallback: Risk 1: wrong AI matches, such as a hallucinated order total, two customers paying the same amount, or a nickname mismatch. Plan: rules run first; the AI sees only leftovers; output must follow a strict JSON schema; a validator rejects any suggestion whose cited bank-line or chat IDs do not exist or whose amount differs from the line; duplicate amounts always go to a human; precision and recall are measured on a labelled 300-line synthetic set before the demo. Risk 2: LLM latency or outage on stage. Fallback: cached LLM outputs for the demo set, plus a rules-only mode that still completes the whole journey, just with a larger exception queue. Risk 3: data access. We do not assume a live Malaysian bank API (not verified). CSV or e-statement upload is the base path and is realistic today, and WhatsApp Business API access is roadmap, with chat-export JSON in the demo. Risk 4: owners not uploading. A weekly reminder, plus forwarding an e-statement PDF by WhatsApp (roadmap).
ideas.business_model: Freemium on Orbyte's credit wallet. Free up to about 50 lines a month, mirroring Bukku's free tier of 50 recommended transactions a month so micro owners can try it at no cost. After that, credits per locked week or per 100 lines. Our price hypothesis is RM10-RM25 a month equivalent; Orbyte publishes no RM prices, so this must be validated. Partner channel: bookkeeping and accounting firms pay per client for clean, locked ledgers (B2B2B), and onboard their micro clients. Later: an owner-consented history pack sent to financing-referral partners through Orbyte Connect, with a disclosed referral fee, where the owner chooses the lender. The growth path runs from week-1 value (finding missing deposits) to a monthly habit to a financing-ready history.

ideas.name: Sedia: monthly lender-ready pack with consent-gated release
ideas.one_liner: Sedia is a rules-only monthly close. It checks a small firm's hub data against the documents banks publicly ask for (BNM SRF FAQ, Oct 2026). It builds the reconciliations, the debtor and creditor ageing and the stock-movement summary, and shows exactly what is missing and who must fix it. Only after the owner signs consent does it release a time-limited pack to a named financier through Orbyte Connect.
ideas.target_user: Small firms (roughly 5-30 staff in services, 5-75 in manufacturing) and micro firms that already have a separate business account. They keep records across an accounting tool, POS, spreadsheets and the bank. An owner or admin clerk scrambles to assemble documents whenever a bank, a grant or a big customer asks. The best fit is goods traders and contractors with credit customers and stock. Their external accountant is a secondary user. Context: BNM (The Star, 30 Jul 2026) describes 'the thin-file segment, which typically lacks an established business track record', and KRI/MDEC (May 2026) says micro firms 'often lack separate business banking and structured systems', which can place them 'outside standard eligibility for financing ... that require formal documentation'.
ideas.trigger: (1) Scheduled: on the 5th of each month, a 'close last month' rule run. (2) Event: the owner presses 'Start financing pack', picks a requirement template and enters a target amount and date. Synthetic example: Kedai Perkakasan Seri Teratai Sdn Bhd (fictional), a building-materials trader in Klang with 9 staff, selling to renovation contractors on 30-day terms. On 20 Oct 2026 its supplier sends a WhatsApp: 'Lim boss, 1 Nov cement & steel price naik 8%. Nak lock order sekarang? Min order RM60k.' A Chinese-speaking supplier writes: '林老板，下个月水泥涨价，要不要先订货？' Owner Mr Lim Wei Kiat (fictional) wants RM60,000 of working capital before 1 Nov, so he opens Sedia.
ideas.connected_data: All data is synthetic in the demo. (a) Accounting system of record via Connect: sales invoices, purchase bills, payment terms, monthly ledger totals (JSON). (b) Business bank statements, 12 months (CSV). (c) POS cash sales (Connect 'e-commerce and POS' category). (d) Month-end stock count spreadsheet and purchases. (e) Orbyte Clients (contractor master with credit terms), org roles, and eSign. (f) Requirement templates as versioned JSON. Each template cites its public source and date. The seed template follows BNM SRF FAQ Q10: 'Bank statements and transaction records', 'Account conduct data (i.e. CCRIS)', 'Audited financial statements or management accounts', 'Sales records, invoices, purchase orders', and 'Stock movement records, and debtor or creditor ageing reports'. (g) Optional: an Asing ledger for firms without a separate account.
ideas.decision_logic: Deterministic and versioned; no AI in any decision. R1 coverage: for each document type, the months on hand against the months the template requires. The demo uses 6 months for bank statements, labelled as an assumption until a lender confirms it. R2 sales-to-bank: invoiced plus POS sales against credits into the business account, per month. A gap above 10% is flagged with the standard explanations to confirm (cash not banked, payments into a personal account, timing). R3 debtor ageing: buckets 0-30, 31-60, 61-90 and over 90 days, from invoice due dates and receipts, with a concentration flag when one customer holds more than 30% of debtors. R4 creditor ageing, built the same way. R5 stock movement: opening stock plus purchases minus cost of goods sold, compared with the closing count. A variance above 5% is flagged. R6 management accounts: the monthly summary must be prepared by the admin and signed off by the owner (accountant review is optional). R7 personal-in-business: transfers to the owner's own name with no drawings entry are flagged. R8 gaps: each gap becomes a task with a role and a due date (target date minus 3 working days). Output: '7 of 9 items ready', with each item red, amber or green and the rule and source rows that decided it. There is never a credit score or an approval probability. Synthetic run: August bank statement missing (red); September stock variance 6.3% (amber, needs a note); debtors RM74,900, of which RM18,400 are over 60 days across 3 contractors (shown, not judged).
ideas.where_ai_adds_value: AI is not needed for the core, and the absence is deliberate. Every check is arithmetic, a date comparison or a lookup. Lenders, accountants and owners need each flag to be reproducible (same input, same output) and explainable to the source rows, which rules guarantee and an LLM does not. The only optional AI, off by default and on the roadmap, would read scanned bank-statement PDFs into rows, with every extracted row shown to the admin for confirmation before any rule uses it.
ideas.why_not_a_chatbot: It has no conversational interface and generates no free text that decides anything. It is a scheduled close plus a checklist engine. It produces reconciliation tables, ageing tables, a completeness checklist with assigned tasks, a signed consent and a revocable, watermarked share link. Judges can see the pitch's restraint: AI is left out where determinism matters.
ideas.human_approval: (1) Monthly close. The admin clerk prepares the close; the owner signs off 'September 2026 closed'. He sees the management summary (synthetic: sales RM186,400; debtors RM74,900 with RM18,400 over 60 days; stock variance 2.1%; sales-to-bank gap 3.4%) and every amber item with the clerk's explanation. (2) Release, the consequential action. Only the owner or director can release the pack. The release screen shows the recipient (picked from the Connect financing-referral partners or entered manually) and the template used ('BNM SRF FAQ Q10 list, Oct 2026'). It shows every file with its months covered, and the third-party personal data included (for example '23 contractor names in debtor ageing', with a 'mask individual names' toggle). It also shows the link expiry (14 days), the watermark text and a revoke button. The owner signs the consent through Orbyte eSign; until then nothing leaves the hub. (3) Revoke. The owner can kill a link at any time.
ideas.roles_and_permissions: All roles are simulated RBAC. Owner/director: sees everything; approves the monthly close; approves and revokes releases; edits templates and thresholds; has a private folder for their own IC and CCRIS report. Admin/finance clerk (Aini): imports data, resolves gaps, writes variance notes, prepares the close and drafts packs. Cannot release, cannot edit templates, and cannot open the owner's private folder. External accountant (KC Tan & Associates, fictional): reads monthly summaries and reconciliations, comments, and marks 'reviewed'. This is not an audit opinion, and the accountant cannot release. Financier (external): view-only, watermarked access to the released pack until it expires; every view is logged. Other staff: no access.
ideas.outcome_and_log: Before the pack is ready, the owner sees: 'Working-capital pack RM60,000: 7/9 ready. Missing: Aug bank statement (Aini, due 28 Oct). Sept stock variance 6.3% needs note (Aini).' After it is ready and released: 'Pack 9/9 complete against BNM SRF FAQ Q10 template. Released to [financier] 25 Oct 2026 10:42, expires 8 Nov, viewed 2 times.' The month view also shows the ageing tables, which put the RM18,400 overdue receivables in front of the owner. The activity log records: each rule run (template version, rule versions, input file hashes, results); each gap created or resolved (who, when, evidence file); each monthly sign-off; each pack generated (file list and hashes); consent signed (eSign reference); release, each view, and expiry or revocation.
ideas.measurable_benefit: These are estimates, and the money link is indirect. (1) Speed to complete documentation: the BNM SRF FAQ (Oct 2026) says banks aim to approve 'within 7 business days, upon receiving complete documentation from SMEs'. Completeness is the gate Sedia controls. Our estimate is that a pack goes from days of chasing documents (a hypothesis to validate with 3-5 owners or clerks) to under 1 hour once monthly closes are current. (2) Money (synthetic illustration only): Lim's 8% supplier increase on a RM60,000 order is RM4,800 he avoids if funds land before 1 Nov. (3) Cash visibility: the monthly debtor ageing surfaces overdue receivables (synthetic: RM18,400 over 60 days) that the owner can chase, and this feeds P1. (4) Accountant cost: management accounts are no longer rebuilt in a rush on request. That saving is not quantified because the fee evidence is weak (Mishu 2021: 'around RM5,000 a year' for outsourced accounting). (5) Accuracy: 100% of flags are reproducible and traceable to the source rows and rule version, and zero releases happen without signed consent. Relevant SDGs: 8.3 (MSME formalisation and access to financial services), 8.2 and 9.3 (access of small enterprises to financial services). Note: the SME SRF itself is limited to SMEs 'materially affected' by the Middle East trade disruptions and runs until 30 Jun 2027. The template is therefore pitched as one example of a published bank document list, not as the target facility for every SME.
ideas.orbyte_fit_and_reuse: It reuses Orbyte's review and approval with audit trail and its roles. It uses eSign (Documenso-based, with an audit log) for owner consent and Clients and Projects for the debtor master. It connects through the Connect categories 'accounting and payroll', 'e-commerce and POS', 'payments and collections' and, for the recipient, 'financing referral'. It is the lender-facing output of Orbyte's stated Business Graph (projects, invoices, payment terms, cash flow). Reusable building block: an Evidence Pack engine where the requirement templates are configuration, so the same engine serves a bank facility, a government-scheme facility, a grant application, a supplier trade-credit application, a tender prequalification or a landlord's request. Sector rule packs: goods (stock rules on), services (stock off, project-billing checks on), F&B (POS-heavy reconciliation). Proposed API: GET /packs/{id}/checklist, and POST /packs/{id}/release, which requires an owner approval token. It stacks with Asing: micro firms without a separate account use Asing's locked ledger as their transaction source.
ideas.scope_check: Not HR or admin. No lending decision, credit score, approval probability, or advice on which facility or lender to choose. Templates only restate the lender's own published list, with the source and date shown. It submits nothing to any bank or government portal on the owner's behalf: release is an owner-approved, revocable share link. It does not pull CCRIS or any credit bureau data; it only reminds the owner to get their own report. No statutory filing and no payments. PDPA 2010: the demo uses synthetic data only. In real use, debtor and creditor lists hold third-party personal data (sole-proprietor contractors), so disclosure happens only with the owner's signed consent, to a named recipient, for a stated purpose (Disclosure principle). An option masks individual names to the minimum necessary. Links are time-limited, watermarked and revocable. Every view is logged. Access is role-based, and the owner's personal documents sit in an owner-only folder (Security). Retention is configurable, and released copies expire (Retention).
ideas.prelim_demo_scope: One live journey on 6 months of synthetic Seri Teratai data. The owner presses 'Start financing pack'. The rules engine shows 7/9 with the reason for each gap. The clerk uploads the missing August statement and adds a stock-variance note. The engine re-runs and shows 9/9. The owner opens the release screen with the third-party data summary and masking toggle, and signs the consent. The demo then shows the generated pack (ZIP or PDF), the share link and the activity log. The single most important feature is the rule-based completeness checklist with explained, assigned gaps, ending in the owner-only release gate.
ideas.hardest_risk_and_fallback: Risk 1: lender requirements are not standardised, so a 'ready' badge could mislead. Plan: the wording is 'complete against [template, source, date]', never 'approved' or 'eligible'. Templates are editable per lender, each cites its public source (the seed is BNM SRF FAQ Q10, Oct 2026), and we validate them with 2-3 bank SME officers or financing-referral partners. Risk 2: messy imports from spreadsheets and different bank formats. Fallback: fixed CSV templates plus a column-mapping screen, and a synthetic-data generator in the repo so the demo never depends on a live system. Risk 3: financing demand is episodic, so owners may not use it monthly. Plan: the monthly close is the recurring hook (ageing and overdue cash every month), and the run happens on schedule even if nobody acts, showing red items. Risk 4: the money link is indirect, as the verifier noted. Plan: lead the pitch with the overdue-receivables and supplier-price story and present financing as the payoff, not the only benefit.
ideas.business_model: Freemium on Orbyte credits: the monthly close checklist is free, to build the habit. Credits are charged per pack generated and per release. Partner model: financiers or financing-referral partners pay a disclosed fee per complete, consented pack they receive. This is a lead-quality fee: the owner always chooses the recipient, and the fee never changes which lenders are shown. Accountant firms pay for a multi-client dashboard that shows which clients are close-current. Growth path: from bank templates to grant, tender and trade-credit templates contributed through Orbyte's planned marketplace.

scores.idea_key: P1-1: Kutip: Cash-Gap Collections Planner
scores.comment: Best fit with Orbyte's own roadmap ('follow up unpaid invoices', Business Graph). Ranking chases against dated payroll and supplier outflows is a real differentiator from Bukku and Xero reminders. Rules-only is the correct choice and is clearly justified. The five-step journey maps exactly to the brief and is cheap to demo live. Innovation is capped because automated reminders already exist. Demand risk is real: nothing shows reminders shorten collection, and corporate or GLC payers pay on their own cycles. The credit-hold rule and the cash-gap meter carry the novelty.

scores.idea_key: P4-2: Pasar Radar: AI supplier price inbox that turns WhatsApp price lists and chits into an approved buy plan
scores.comment: AI earns its place: code-mixed supplier price messages, local pack units and handwritten chits really do defeat regex. Rules make every buying decision and the owner approves each order. The burden recurs daily, procurement is clear white space for Orbyte, and the schema generalises to hardware, auto parts and manufacturing. The two-sided supplier play is a credible growth story. Weaknesses: savings are modest (RM15.80 a day, synthetic) and rest on multiple suppliers quoting the same items. Supplier relationships and credit terms may outweigh a few sen. Cash wet-market buys have no message to read.

scores.idea_key: P5-1: VO Catcher: WhatsApp site instructions to signed variation confirmations
scores.comment: The most original concept. Turning WhatsApp site instructions into BQ-priced variation orders that the main contractor e-signs is a specific, money-relevant pain. AI is used narrowly for classification and extraction; rules do the pricing. It reuses Orbyte eSign and Projects well, and the scope boundary (no CIPAA notices, no legal advice) is disciplined. The demo is visually strong. Risks: it is one vertical, and the claim that it generalises to 'change requests' is still a roadmap promise. Precision and recall on code-mixed site chat are unproven. Micro-firm evidence is thin, and no source shows how often missing documents lose disputes.

scores.idea_key: P3-1: SahBayar Gate: payment-verified release for orders
scores.comment: Very clear story. The storekeeper's button stays red while the lorry waits, and separation of duties is the product. Rules-only matching against actual credits beats every fake-receipt trick without judging images, which is elegant and explainable. It targets the narrower segment that survived verification (staff-released B2B orders), not hawkers. Weaknesses: the credit feed is a manual CSV upload or owner confirmation, with no verified open-banking route. It competes with payment links and soundboxes. Per-business loss frequency is unproven.

scores.idea_key: P4-1: MarginGuard (Harga Bukti): per-dish cost-to-price check with a dated cost-evidence log
scores.comment: Smart reframe around KPDN Section 21 and the dated cost-evidence pack, which turns a soft 'see your margin' pitch into one with a regulatory hook. Pure arithmetic, so rules-only is right. Portion, substitute and hold are treated as equal levers, which respects owners' real limits on pricing power. It generalises via bill-of-materials templates. Weaknesses: recipe and BOM setup is a real adoption barrier for micro F&B. There is no evidence micro owners pay for costing, and wet-market buys have no receipts.

scores.idea_key: P1-2: Bukti: WhatsApp Payment-Proof & Promise Reconciler
scores.comment: Strong 'AI extracts, rules decide' design with a hard guard: no PAID status without a matching bank line. It mirrors eClaim on the money-in side. The deduction-to-DO linkage and the parsing of promised dates are genuinely useful for logistics and wholesale. Weaknesses: the journey is harder to explain cold. It depends on a vision LLM plus a bank CSV. It overlaps with TutupKira and Kutip; it would be stronger merged into one receivables suite than pitched as a separate preliminary idea.

scores.idea_key: P2-1: TempahLock: order commitment gate (rules only)
scores.comment: Clean rules engine with thoughtful false-positive handling: no deposit rule for government buyers, verification through ePerolehan or a callback instead. Easy to build. The core problem remains: the money is lost in a bank app the product cannot touch. In a one-to-four-person firm the owner who approves is the same person being deceived, so the gate is largely advisory. Fraud hits any one firm rarely, so daily value depends on the order-book side, which overlaps free tools such as Take App.

scores.idea_key: P3-2: TutupKira AI: nightly claimed-vs-received close
scores.comment: Reasonable use of AI to read screenshots from many layouts and link messy chat to bank lines. Fraud judgement is rightly left to the bank credit. Detecting the problem next day rather than months later is a clear benefit. But it largely duplicates Bukti and SahBayar's reconciliation engine. Hawkers and bazaar targets are unlikely buyers of a team hub, and it still depends on a manual bank CSV. It is better as the detection tier of SahBayar than as a standalone pitch.

scores.comment: unused

scores.idea_key: P1-1: Kutip: Cash-Gap Collections Planner
scores.comment: Persona: owner of a 4-person printing shop in Seri Kembangan who sells on 60-day terms. I chase payment every week and payroll keeps me awake. 'Short RM2,000 for payroll on 31 Oct, chase these 3 first' speaks my language, and the wa.me prefilled message in BM/中文 means my clerk can do the nudging without me. I can explain it to staff in 2 minutes. Reminders alone are not new (Bukku does email ones), but ranking against my payroll date plus the credit-hold card is. It stops working if I must retype every invoice; CSV or Sheet import is a must. Would pay RM30-40/month, less than Bukku Grow.

scores.idea_key: P1-2: Bukti: WhatsApp Payment-Proof & Promise Reconciler
scores.comment: Persona: owner of a 14-person haulage firm in Klang with one account clerk. My clerk really does lose hours matching 'dah bank in boss' slips and deductions to trips, and short-payments get forgotten until year-end. Linking a RM330 deduction to the DO is useful. But it needs me to upload the bank statement daily, and the customer has to send slips to one number, not the group chat. It saves clerk time, not new cash. Too much for a micro firm. Would pay RM50-80/month if it truly cuts 10 clerk-hours.

scores.idea_key: P2-1: TempahLock: order commitment gate (rules only)
scores.comment: Persona: owner of a 4-person kuih and catering business in Ipoh. I know the fake 'PPD' order scam and it is scary. But I am the one taking orders at 9pm, so the gate mostly gates me. Keeping a catalogue alias list, an approved supplier list and a 'second key' person is too much setup for us. The deposit rule I already enforce by habit. I would switch it on near Raya as insurance, not use it every week. Would pay RM10-15/month, and only in festive season.

scores.idea_key: P2-2: LO Lens: AI reader for government and bulk order bundles
scores.comment: Persona: owner of a 3-person printing and stationery shop in Temerloh that sells to schools and PPD. One fake LO could wipe out my savings, so the 'call the official number, not the one in the message' card is valuable. But I get maybe 2-3 LOs a month, so it is an occasional tool. The directory of official agency numbers is the part I actually want. Would pay per check, around RM5 a bundle, or RM10-20/month at most.

scores.idea_key: P3-1: SahBayar Gate: payment-verified release for orders
scores.comment: Persona: owner of a 9-person frozen food wholesaler in Klang. My storekeeper loads lorries on screenshots and only I see the bank account, so a red 'Jangan muat barang' button fixes a real gap. Staff understand red and green in a minute. The weak spot is me uploading a bank CSV several times a day while the lorry waits. If the owner tap 'seen in bank app' is quick on my phone, I would use it daily. Would pay RM40-60/month.

scores.idea_key: P3-2: TutupKira AI: nightly claimed-vs-received close
scores.comment: Persona: owner of a 6-person bakery in Seremban with resellers. The morning card ('4 issues RM737, Liza agent RM640 not in') is the kind of thing I would read with my coffee. Catching a dishonest agent in days, not months, is worth money. But my staff will not reliably forward every screenshot, and exporting chats each night is a chore. Detection after the goods have gone is weaker than blocking at release. Would pay RM25-35/month.

scores.idea_key: P4-1: MarginGuard (Harga Bukti): per-dish cost-to-price check with a dated cost-evidence log
scores.comment: Persona: owner of a 6-person kopitiam in Bangi. I know sawi went up; I do not need software to tell me. What I cannot do is raise prices without customers running away. Setting up recipe grams for 40 dishes is a nightmare; my cook does not measure. The KPDN evidence log is the most interesting part, but I would only need it if KPDN came knocking. Would pay RM15-20/month, honestly more likely free tier only.

scores.idea_key: P4-2: Pasar Radar: AI supplier price inbox that turns WhatsApp price lists and chits into an approved buy plan
scores.comment: Persona: owner of a 4-person catering kitchen in Shah Alam buying from 3 suppliers daily. Not retyping three messy price lists every night is nice, and splitting the order to save RM15 a day adds up to about RM400 a month. But I keep my usual supplier for credit terms and reliability, so I would untick most switches. Many small kopitiams have only one or two suppliers, so the comparison is thin. Would pay RM20-30/month if savings show up in the first month.

scores.idea_key: P5-1: VO Catcher: WhatsApp site instructions to signed variation confirmations
scores.comment: Persona: owner of a 9-person M&E subcontractor. This is exactly how I lose money: the site supervisor says 'tambah 2 power point' on WhatsApp, we do it, and at claim time nobody remembers or the main con denies it. Turning the chat into a priced VO list with my BQ rate before the claim cut-off is new to me and pays for itself after one VO. Risk: the main contractor may never click the eSign link, and the AI must catch Manglish site slang. Would pay RM50-80 per active project/month.

scores.idea_key: P5-2: HoldBack Ledger: claim-to-cash, retention release and exposure tracker
scores.comment: Persona: owner of a 14-person aluminium and glass subcontractor running 4 projects. I do forget to claim the second half of retention after DLP, and RM10k is real money. The 'money stuck per main contractor' view is useful. But my Excel already does most of this if my admin is disciplined, and Bukku handles retention invoices. Would pay RM30-40/month, more if bundled with VO Catcher.

scores.idea_key: P7-1: Tempoh: a cross-agency obligation engine with threshold watch and professional hand-off
scores.comment: Persona: owner-director of a 14-person aircond services Sdn Bhd. My company secretary already reminds me about SSM, and my accountant handles SST. Most of these deadlines are yearly, so I would open it maybe 5 times a year. Joining tenancy stamping and the DBKL licence into one view is mildly handy, but it is not a weekly tool and not a money-maker. Would pay RM10-15/month, more likely nothing.

scores.idea_key: P7-2: Surat Masuk: an AI reader that turns official documents into verified deadlines
scores.comment: Persona: owner of a 4-person nasi campur shop in Setapak. Snapping the DBKL notice and getting 'pay by 4 Nov, licence renewal blocked until settled' is easy to understand. But I get an official letter maybe once every few months, so I would forget the app exists. Unpaid compounds blocking licence renewal is the useful insight. Would pay RM5-10/month, or per document only.

scores.idea_key: P8-1: Asing: business/personal money splitter for owner-run firms
scores.comment: Persona: solo home baker in Shah Alam using one personal account for everything. Finding the RM120 deposit Lina 'already transferred' but never sent is real money, and my accountant would stop nagging me. But uploading a bank CSV every Sunday and exporting chats is homework I will skip after week 3. The financing-history payoff is too far away to motivate me. Would pay RM10-15/month.

scores.idea_key: P8-2: Sedia: monthly lender-ready pack with consent-gated release
scores.comment: Persona: owner of a 9-person building materials trader in Klang. I apply for financing maybe once every year or two, and my accountant pulls the documents. The debtor ageing each month is useful, but my accounting software already shows it. The monthly close checklist feels like more admin, not less. Would pay per pack, around RM50 when I need a loan, and close to RM0/month otherwise.

P1-2: Bukti: WhatsApp Payment-Proof & Promise Reconciler

owner.biggest_concern: Most ideas need the owner to keep feeding the tool, by uploading bank CSVs, keeping catalogues and recipes up to date, or forwarding every screenshot. Busy micro owners stop doing this within weeks. The ideas that survive are the ones that work on data the owner already has, such as an invoice list or a site chat, and that give back visible ringgit fast.

scores.idea_key: P1-1: Kutip: Cash-Gap Collections Planner
scores.comment: Most buildable full journey here: CSV in, 08:00 scan, ranked chase plan, owner approves a Tier 2 message, clerk logs a payment, the gap meter closes, log updates. All rules, so it is deterministic on stage. A 2-person team can do it in 2 days. Wow moment: 'Short RM2,000 for payroll 31 Oct' turns green after the RM3,180 payment. Matches Orbyte's own stated roadmap item ('follow up unpaid invoices'), which is the strongest hub-fit argument in the set. Weakness: judges may say 'Bukku/Xero already send reminders'. The cash-gap prioritisation and credit hold must lead the pitch, not the reminders. The demand risk (no evidence reminders shorten collection) is honestly named, and the wa.me fallback is credible. Leaving AI out is defensible, but it caps innovation.

scores.idea_key: P1-2: Bukti: WhatsApp Payment-Proof & Promise Reconciler
scores.comment: Best AI-justified idea. A code-mixed message ('Got deduct RM330 for 2 pallet tiles pecah at Bukit Raja') plus a slip becomes a 3-invoice allocation with the deduction linked to DO-8812. Judges will remember that. AI only extracts, rules decide, and M1 (never PAID without a bank line) makes it safe to demo live. Vision LLMs read clean synthetic slips reliably, and the cached JSON fallback covers latency. Risks: the scope is wider than it looks (allocation combinatorics, deduction linking, relative-date resolution, POD role). The team must hard-cut to the one Mega Bina scenario. Building fictional slip layouts takes time. Clear Orbyte eClaim analogue, and it pairs naturally with Kutip as a roadmap.

scores.idea_key: P4-2: Pasar Radar: AI supplier price inbox that turns WhatsApp price lists and chits into an approved buy plan
scores.comment: Text extraction from 3 short supplier messages is the most reliable LLM task in the whole set, so it is low-risk live. Wow moment: three messy messages in BM, Manglish and Chinese collapse into one unit-normalised comparison grid, with the cili spike flagged and per-supplier order messages generated, including one in Chinese. The AI value is obvious and not a chatbot. Weakness: the headline saving (RM15.80/day) is small, and relationship and credit-term loyalty may dominate switching, so pitch spike detection and time saved too. The handwritten chit is a stretch; drop it if OCR is flaky. Hub fit is plausible (procurement white space) but less tied to Orbyte's stated roadmap.

scores.idea_key: P4-1: MarginGuard (Harga Bukti): per-dish cost-to-price check with a dated cost-evidence log
scores.comment: Pure arithmetic rules with seeded recipes, so it is nearly impossible to break on stage. Wow moment: one sawi price entry turns a dish red with a 'RM600/month leak' and four costed levers, then an exportable KPDN Section 21 evidence pack. That evidence pack is a genuinely original angle and gives the pain a deadline hook. Clear consequential approval (a POS price change). Risks: real-world recipe setup (named, with a 'top 10 dishes' fallback) and pricing power (handled by not pushing price rises). The verifier showed the SMEAM headline stats are about wages, so do not quote them.

scores.idea_key: P5-1: VO Catcher: WhatsApp site instructions to signed variation confirmations
scores.comment: Strong two-pane demo: WhatsApp bubbles on the left, priced VO cards with BQ matches on the right, then PM fixes a quantity, owner approves, eSign is mocked. It reuses Orbyte eSign, which is good fit evidence. The AI does real work (classifying instruction vs coordination vs hold, '3-05 sampai 3-08 x2 = 8'). Risks: classification and recall on code-mixed site chat are less reliable than plain extraction. Without the 60-80 message labelled set, the accuracy claim is hollow. Construction is a niche the team may not understand; judges may probe CIPAA. Micro-firm evidence is thin. Feasible for a team with someone comfortable with prompt plus eval.

scores.idea_key: P3-1: SahBayar Gate: payment-verified release for orders
scores.comment: Very buildable state machine. The 'storekeeper button stays red while the lorry waits' moment is vivid, and the 1-sen trick showing 'SHORT RM311.99' is a nice beat. Separation of duties is a real, explainable control. But the pain is narrow: soundboxes and payment links already solve most of it. A credit feed that depends on manual CSV upload creates real-world friction at pickup time, which judges will spot. Good backup choice; weaker market story than the top 5.

scores.idea_key: P2-2: LO Lens: AI reader for government and bulk order bundles
scores.comment: Memorable demo: the LO shows a gmail address and a mobile number against the directory's landline, and 'pembekal panel kami' is highlighted as a known scam tactic. Big per-incident losses make the story emotional. The 'AI can only raise the bar, never lower it' principle is good. But fraud hits any one firm rarely, so there is little daily value, and the gate is advisory because money moves in the bank app. Tactic detection on 15 self-made bundles invites the 'you tested on your own data' critique. The synthetic agency directory is fine for the demo, but its production upkeep is a hidden cost.

scores.idea_key: P3-2: TutupKira AI: nightly claimed-vs-received close
scores.comment: A nice morning card ('4 isu RM737') and real AI value in reading many slip layouts and screen types (request-for-money vs success). But producing about 30 convincing synthetic screenshots across fictional banks is a large asset-making job for a short hackathon. It largely overlaps Bukti and SahBayar, and it is detection after the fact rather than a consequential approval, which makes the approval step feel soft. Pick Bukti instead if going AI on slips.

scores.idea_key: P2-1: TempahLock: order commitment gate (rules only)
scores.comment: Easy to build and clear: a fake PPD order is HELD with 4 plain reasons, the RM9,000 supplier prepay is blocked by two keys plus a cooling-off. The thoughtful touch is dropping the deposit rule for government buyers. Weak spots: rare per-business incidence, so it works like insurance. The owner being deceived is usually the approver. The daily value (deposit discipline) is already handled by Take App and simple policy. Judges may see it as a checklist.

scores.idea_key: P8-1: Asing: business/personal money splitter for owner-run firms
scores.comment: Real niche (commingled accounts, thin-file financing), and the bank line beside chat bubble exception queue is a decent demo. But matching across bank narrative, e-wallet and chats with many classes is the hardest AI pipeline here. The 300-line labelled set is heavy for a few days. The money link is indirect, and the pain was verified as weak (e-invoice hook gone). Overlaps Bukti/TutupKira matching. Better as a roadmap data layer.

scores.idea_key: P5-2: HoldBack Ledger: claim-to-cash, retention release and exposure tracker
scores.comment: Deterministic and testable with a date simulator, so it is safe live. But the wow moment is just alerts landing in an inbox. Bukku already does retention receivable and reminders, which the team admits. Construction-niche knowledge is required to pitch it credibly. Best kept as VO Catcher's roadmap companion, not as the lead.

scores.idea_key: P7-2: Surat Masuk: an AI reader that turns official documents into verified deadlines
scores.comment: A DBKL notice photo turning into a deadline plus 'licence renewal BLOCKED' is a neat beat, and extraction with human date confirmation is demo-safe. But document frequency per firm is unevidenced, and the domain reads as admin and compliance, which risks the 'overlaps Orbyte admin' critique. The pain verification for P7 was close to refuted for micro firms.

scores.idea_key: P8-2: Sedia: monthly lender-ready pack with consent-gated release
scores.comment: Rules are fine, but there are 8 of them across reconciliation, ageing and stock, which is a lot of data modelling for a checklist outcome. The wow moment is just '7/9 becomes 9/9'. Financing demand is episodic, the money link is indirect, and the SRF template applies only to SMEs affected by the Middle East disruption. Consent-gated release is good PDPA practice but not compelling as the core.

scores.idea_key: P7-1: Tempoh: a cross-agency obligation engine with threshold watch and professional hand-off
scores.comment: Verifiers judged this close to refuted for micro firms: the obligations are annual and company secretaries already own them. Sourcing and versioning even 8 rules correctly is error-prone, and one wrong date on stage would be fatal. It is close to the admin/compliance territory the brief warns against. The rule-change re-compute demo is clever but does not rescue the weak pain.

builder.biggest_concern: Every pain behind these ideas verified at only 2/4, and the benefit figures (owner hours, collection days cut, RM saved) are team assumptions, not evidence. A university team with synthetic data risks a polished demo resting on unproven demand. They must run 3-5 owner interviews before the final, and pitch measured process metrics rather than invented RM savings. Secondary concern: four ideas (Bukti, TutupKira, SahBayar, Asing) depend on the same slip-plus-bank-CSV matching core and the same unavailable WhatsApp/bank APIs. The team should pick one, scope it to a single scenario with cached AI fallback, and treat the rest as roadmap. Bukti fronted by Kutip's rules is the strongest combined story, because it fits Orbyte's stated roadmap.
